INTRODUCTION

Ambrosiaster was an anonymous fourth century Christian writer who is credited with writing commentaries on all of St. Paul’s epistles and a compilation of treatises known as the Questions on the Old and New Testaments.  The name Ambrosiaster is not the actual name of the writer, but the name means “Star of Ambrose,” and this name was given after the Ambrosian authorship of the commentaries on Paul’s epistles had been ruled out, which will be discussed further below.  Scholars are still unsure of the author’s identity, but they are certain that the same author is responsible for both the commentaries on the epistles and the Questions.

These Questions (Quaestio) means ‘an enquiry’ or investigation into passages of Scripture which are difficult to understand.1 The Questions on the Old and New Testaments is a compilation of essays of various sizes as well as discourses and sermons.  Some of the questions thoroughly examine and explain important doctrinal matters such as the meaning of God, the sin of Adam and Eve, baptism of the Savior, etc.  Some questions are treatises against opponents to Christianity and heretics such as Pagans, Arians, Novatian, etc. There are some questions that are running commentaries on the Psalms and Gospels, while others are on Old Testament heroes such as Melchizedek, Abraham, Job, and Tobit.2   

The Questions by Ambrosiaster are found in two different manuscript traditions.  Both manuscript traditions are displayed in this translation and placed in sections or categories, such as, 1st Category and 2nd Category.  The manuscript tradition of the 1st Category is a compilation of 127 “Questions” and the MS tradition of the 2nd Category is a compilation of 150. “Of these questions, eighty-nine are common to both collections, and almost two thirds of these eighty-nine have undergone some rewriting.”3   The English translation for this book is based upon the text from the collection of Migne (PL 35 2214-2416).

There are a lot of explanations to specific passages of Scripture in the Questions by Ambrosiaster, which means that they are useful for exegetical purposes.  The way that the questions are organized in the manuscripts and the printed edition that this translation is based upon would make it difficult, to say the least, to use it for looking up specific passages to see what Ambrosiaster had to say about them, because the order of the questions in the manuscripts do not follow a consistent pattern nor order that the Scripture passages would be in the Bible. For this reason, I have chosen to provide the questions that concern specific passages of Scripture to follow the order found in the Bible, such as by book, chapter, and verse.  For those questions that are polemic in nature, they are placed in a section separate called “Polemic,” and other questions that are not polemic nor exegetical are placed in a section called “Miscellaneous.”

For many years, the Questions on the Old and New Testaments were thought to have been written by Augustine of Hippo and were placed among his works.  Scholars have long determined since then that it was not written by Augustine, and was in fact the same author of the Bible commentaries of Paul’s epistles that is mentioned above.  There are many examples that demonstrate how scholarly rejection of the Augustinian authorship of the Questions is more than justified, starting with the choice of topics, the method of teaching, the difference of style, which are quite in opposition to the genius and the faith of Augustine.  Augustine’s teachings on original sin is an indicator that he was not the author of the Questions, because the author claims without constraint, in Question 13, that the children who died with their parents in the fire of Sodom were “exempt from the punishments of hell, because they have been victims of a crime they did not commit.” Therefore, the author of these questions has appeared here to deny ‘original sin.’  Also, the same author claims, in questions 21 and 45, that ‘woman’ was not created in the image of God, while St. Augustine teaches the contrary in his book on the Literal Meaning of Genesis, Book 3, chapter 22.  Another example, in question 41, the author endeavors to prove that these words of Genesis: "The Spirit of God was carried on the waters," should not be understood of the Holy Spirit, as Augustine, however, explains it in several places.4

As mentioned above, scholars are of the opinion, for good reason, that the authorship of the Questions on the Old and New Testaments is the same for the Bible commentaries on the epistles of Paul.5 Alexander Souter, who devoted nearly 130 pages to this point, demonstrated by comparing these two works and found the greatest similarities between the community of illustrations and allusions, comparison of Scripture quotations, comparison of style and language, identity of thought such as favorite texts of Scripture and interpretations of Scripture.6  Scholars think, moreover, that these two works must have been composed at about the same time; the commentaries, under the pontificate of Pope Damasus, who died towards the end of the year 384, as attested by the author of these writings in chapter 3, verse 15 of the second epistle to Timothy, and Question 44 (Against the Jews).7

As mentioned above, scholars are uncertain of the identity of the author of the commentaries and the Questions, but I will leave the readers with a quote from Alexander Souter on this point…

“Erasmus, in the year 1527, was the ﬁrst to suspect the accuracy of this ascription; and thereafter speculation became rife as to the real author. At the dawning of modern scholarship, as it is still more clearly at the present time, Ambrosian authorship was seen to be an impossibility. Some guessed that the work was a cento made from S. Jerome and S. Chrysostom by some unknown person; others believed it to be by Julian of Aeclanum or some other Pelagian; others by Remigius, others by Tyconius, the author of the ‘Rules,’ others by S. Hilary of Poitiers, others by Hilary of Pavia, others by Hilary of Syracuse; very many have attributed the work to Hilarius, a deacon of Rome. The statement of S. Augustine, who undoubtedly meant S. Hilary of Poitiers as the author of the quotation he makes, is responsible for the last four views. S. Hilary of Poitiers is unhesitatingly to be rejected owing to known differences of style. Most of the other names are idle conjectures, carelessly thrown out before the days of exact method in the study of literature and history. Langen himself put forward a view that Faustinus, a Roman presbyter, is the author. His proof, built up chiefly from a comparison of the language of both works with that of the De Tririitate and other writings of Faustinuss, is so far from being convincing that it certainly shows Faustinian authorship to be impossible. This conjecture has had the fate of the others. Dr Marold and Dom Morin, for example, explicitly reject it. The recent view, that Isaac, a converted Jew, who was concerned in the disturbances at the election of Pope Damasus and afterwards relapsed to Judaism, wrote the commentaries and the Quaestiones V. et N. Testamenti, is due to Dom Germain Morin, O.S.B., of the Abbaye, Maredsous, who by his successful researches and independent criticism has shown himself a worthy follower of his Benedictine predecessors. Dr. Zahn and Mr. A. E. Burn, both called for a fuller treatment of the subject. This I have endeavored to supply, as the special study I had devoted to the language of the commentary seemed to invite me to the task. I can heartily support Dom Morin’s second suggestion, that Hilary, the Layman, was the author.”8

QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS

GENESIS

1ST CATEGORY OT

QUESTION 106. ON GENESIS. — In the beginning God made heaven and earth (Gen. 1:1). If He made heaven in the beginning, and the earth, and if heaven is the firmament, as is evident in what follows, then this is not literally true, because light was made first, and therefore the firmament: for it could not signify some other heaven, since it is describing the making of the world as perfected by the working of God. For this reason, because people were misled by various opinions about the cause of the world, Moses, inspired by God, showed what the true ordering of the world was. To some it seemed that it had no beginning; to others that it did have a beginning, but was fashioned by certain Angels; to others again that it was likewise made, but by a certain Saklas, who is also the god of opposing power; but a few, following the path of truth concerning its origin, asserted that God was its maker. Therefore, because of those who were drawn away by false opinions of diversity, Moses was compelled to show what its true cause was, lest the children of Israel, freed from the power of the Egyptians, should still not be released from their false understanding. For they, more than the rest, pursued the study of error: for in ancient times they above others devoted themselves to vain philosophy. Indeed Moses, because he was adopted by Pharaoh’s daughter, is said to have been taught in all the wisdom of the Egyptians (Acts 7:22). What then is the meaning of his words, In the beginning God made heaven and earth? If it signifies the firmament, according to what we showed above, let us see what he says. We think that Moses, so as to remove all error about the lower creation and about the materials of the world’s construction, indicated that in the beginning the very substances from which the world is constituted were made; for if he had kept silence about this, they might perhaps be thought to be eternal substances, considered to be yoked to God. So that the one who receives testimony about this matter cannot doubt that the world was made, since he confesses that the substances which served for the expenditure of the world were subjected in the beginning. Therefore, In the beginning God made heaven and earth, that is, the upper and the lower substance. The upper is that from which heaven consists; the lower, however, is a certain thick dreg-like concretion which advanced into the dry land that is called earth, and into darkness. Therefore He says in the prophet Isaiah, I am God, who made light and created darkness (Isa. 45:6–7). When these were created, He made at the same time the substance, that is, water, darkness, and earth before times: for times are under the firmament. For the firmament, as some think, is the ice of the waters. And it is therefore called firmament, because the waters, being solidified by divine power, are made firm, which, from covering or concealing, is called heaven. And therefore, because water is the greater element, it is mentioned first, since a part of it advanced into the vault of the world. The earth, however, is the pavement: which indeed David, by the Holy Spirit, confesses to have been created. For he says, And the waters that are above the heavens, let them praise the name of the Lord. For He Himself spoke, and they were made; He Himself commanded, and they were created (Ps. 148:4–5). After these elements, before the joining together of the world, God made light, so that His works should go forth in the light, which light, by a fixed arrangement, completed the course of the day. Night came to be according to the measure of the day, which likewise, when the measure of its span was fulfilled, was illumined by the coming of the morning light: and therefore the first day was completed when the second began; for the night is reckoned to the day, so that together they are called one day: for because darkness is subject to light, it lacks authority and cannot make up a number. For thirty days are called one moon, even though nights are included with them. Therefore the service of light, by which it uses up the space assigned to it, is called day. But the substance of darkness, before it is illumined, is called night. And that space which is between the setting and the rising is night. For it is not darkness that makes the night, just as it is not light that makes the day, because darkness remains in its own nature. The coming of light makes day, and its departure makes night. Not without reason, therefore, is the night subject to the day. So, when light was made, and the course of twelve hours completed, and likewise the space of the night of twelve hours also passed, there was an equinox on the first day: and from then the day began to grow longer than the night, namely throughout three months, which are the spring season. From that increase the day then diminishes through three other months, which are the summer season. And again there is an equinox, so that from then the night grows longer than the day through another three months, which are the autumn season. And again the night, from the greatness by which it surpasses the day, begins to diminish until the end of the fourth season, which is winter. And the equinox returns to the first season, when God created the world, which day is understood to be the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, when the first day of Passover is, that is, the first day of the first month. For in the Law it is commanded that on the tenth day of the first month in the evening they should prepare themselves to celebrate Passover on the fourteenth day of the month, that is, from the eleventh. For already the evening of the tenth day shines into the eleventh, so that from the eleventh day before the Kalends of April the beginning of the first month should be. For at the beginning the moon was made on the fourteenth, because all things were made full. Add three days from the evening of the tenth, and these are the three days before the luminaries that were made, so that the world was made on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April; for the number of the moon from the eleventh comes to the fourteenth, to which the first month of Passover in its entirety is assigned, so that on the solemn day of Passover it should be neither beyond the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, nor beyond the fourteenth moon, because the world was made on the eleventh, and on the fourteenth the moon was made brighter with greater light. Between the beginning, therefore, and the brightness with which the world was illumined, our Savior both suffered and rose again; for He suffered on the fourteenth moon, and rose on the first day, which is therefore called the Lord’s Day, because the Lord Himself made it, who made the multiplied months, and the seasons, and the years. And so that it might never be celebrated in exactly the same way, the course of the moon in its wanings and waxings brings this about. But the earth was invisible and unformed. It is clear that the earth, after it was made, was invisible and unformed: for it was covered by waters, and therefore was invisible; and it was unformed because, being fluid, it was not suitable for cultivation. And darkness was upon the abyss. He says that darkness was upon the abyss, that is, upon the boundless water on every side. And the spirit of God was borne above the water (Gen. 1:2). This water he signifies as the extremity, above which the spirit of God, because it was borne above it, shows that the darkness was upon the infinite depth. As for the spirit of God above the waters, since where the spirit of God was, there was no obscurity, it illuminated the water as far as it could. But it could not illuminate the abyss, that is, the immense depth: that is, it illuminated the higher waters, and beneath there was darkness, and over the abyss. He therefore calls this the spirit of God not because he wishes this to be understood as the Holy Spirit, but because he wishes it to be understood spiritually over the material creation, and by calling him the spirit of God who was moving above the waters, he signifies that he is wholly of God, so as to overturn the perverse assertion used by some, who say there is something that is not of God. For it is neither orderly nor reasonable that the Holy Spirit should be said to have been over the waters, since he is over all creation. For whatever is of God is above all powers and principalities and likewise above all spiritual powers. Nor should anyone’s mind be disturbed because he is called the spirit of God, when it is established that all things are God’s. For God, among other things when he was about to make the flood, says: My spirit shall not remain in these men, because they are flesh (Gen. 6:3); and in Ezekiel, among other things: Therefore says the Lord to these bones, I will spread skin over you, and I will give my spirit in you, and you shall live (Ezek. 37:5). Do these things belong to the office of the Holy Spirit, and not to the soul? Therefore this spirit of God is indeed, like the rest, but is the governor of material substances; for his appointed order is to preside over these. When light was made, and the course of day set in order, and the second day completed, he made the firmament, that is, heaven, so that the light in the earth of the firmament might govern the day, so that it might be as a lamp in a house. This firmament, I say, was made from the aforesaid substance of water. For now the world is being joined together in form, so that from the confusion of things, with substances distinguished, individual parts might be fitted which would contribute to the members of the world. For the substances which we said were first made are expended upon the world. And therefore it is called “world” (mundus), because the things that were mixed together, once separated from one another and brought into form, made it called “world,” to whose structure they contributed. Therefore the firmament, that is, heaven, was made in the midst of the waters, so that it might divide between the water that was above the firmament and the water that was below the firmament; so that by God’s power the firmament might stand in the midst of the waters, having water beneath itself, and within itself, and above and around itself; so that it might be concave on the outside and fortified within, lest the waters, whether inner or outer, should penetrate its concavity, so that it might be as a house fortified and strengthened, that those dwelling in it might be secure. On the third day he commanded the water that was under heaven, that is, within the capacity of the firmament, to be gathered into one place, so that the dry land, which is the earth, might appear, and therefore it came to pass. For the breadth of the earth having been drawn out, there was made as it were a basin, in which all the water that was within the firmament might be sunk down, and the dry land appeared. When the water receded, it was necessary that the earth, made visible, should appear, which before had been invisible. Then the dry land was called earth, and the gatherings of the waters seas. And he commanded the earth to bring forth grass for food, and fruit-bearing trees for seed upon the earth. Then on the fourth day God commanded luminaries to be made in the firmament of heaven, that they might shine upon the earth: the greater luminary at the beginning of the day, and the lesser luminary at the beginning of the night, and the stars. These relate to the conception and birth and nourishment of those things which are begotten in the world, and to the signs of seasons needed for fixed intervals, and also to the adornment of the whole world. For just as it belongs to the adornment of a house if its ceiling has panels marked with gold, so also the stars, shining with diverse light, provide adornment to the world. Therefore to the light which was first made, the brightness of the sun is added, so that these are joined and inseparable. And to the night, which was dark, a luminary is given; and because the moon was at the fourteenth day when it was made, therefore he says, The lesser luminary at the beginning of the night: for when it was made, it shone the whole night. From the part, therefore, it is said “at the beginning of the night,” because it does not always shine in the evening. But the greater luminary, which we call the sun, remains at the beginning of the day, because it was compacted together with the prior light. For three days the world existed without these luminaries; for as yet there were not those for whose benefit their functions would serve. But when the earth brought forth grass for food and fruit-bearing trees, there was need of things that would nourish or preserve what had been brought forth. Because all generation of these is completed through their intervention, it was not fitting that these should be made first, lest, by the effect of those things produced from the earth, they should be thought to have arisen; but he made those first, so that therefore these might be without doubt understood to have been made without them. Then on the fifth day he commanded the waters to bring forth creeping things of living souls, and winged creatures flying over the earth beneath the firmament of heaven, and it was so. And among other things, And God saw, he says, that they were good, and he said, Increase and multiply (Gen. 1:21–22). He added, And God saw that they were good, because some say they are evil, so that at least in this way they may feel shame. For when they please God and their maker, surely they ought to displease no one. For fools are accustomed to say, Therefore, they say, he saw, and they pleased him, because previously he did not know. O dull ones, how could He not know? Whatever He willed came forth. Can anyone will what he does not know? And can He who is able to act be said not to know what He is doing? And what is more, He did not make them Himself, but commanded that they be made; and is He who commands not possessed of the power to make? But because all things are possible for Him, when He commanded that what could not do so should begin to be able, it was in order that it might contribute to His praise. There is therefore a double power, that He should command what is insensible to bring forth what is sensible. On the sixth day He commanded the earth to bring forth living soul, quadrupeds, and beasts of the earth; and so it was done, and they were brought forth. And God saw that they were good, and very good, because all are necessary. On the day mentioned above, therefore, God said: Let us make man in our image and likeness, and, He said, let him have power over all things that have been made upon the earth (Gen. 1:26). First indeed God made the substances out of which He would frame the world; when it was compacted, adorned with all its embellishments, and furnished with what was necessary, He then made man, who would enjoy it and all that is in it. For whereas He had commanded that everything on earth should be brought forth from water and earth, yet when He made man, He is described as having taken clay of the earth in His hands, so that He might teach how greatly man differs from the things He had already made. He wishes it to pertain to the honor of man that he is described as being made by the hands of God, and made in the image and likeness of God, that is, of the Father and the Son. What it is to be in the image and likeness of God, although we have said elsewhere, yet this place and its occasion require that we say it again. The words are from the Father to the Son, saying, Let us make man in our image and likeness: although in the work the person of both is understood, of Him who speaks and of Him who hears. This then is the image of God in man, that one man was made as it were a lord, from whom the rest would arise, having the dominion of God as His vicar; for every king bears the image of God. Therefore woman was not made in the image of God. Therefore it says, And God made man; in the image of God He made him. Therefore it is that the Apostle says, A man indeed ought not to cover his head, because he is the image and glory of God; but the woman covers it for this reason, because she is not the glory or image of God (1 Cor. 11:7). The likeness of God in man is this, that just as from the Father is the Son, so from man is woman. In this plainly there is a difference, because she was made, whereas He was born. Yet to some it seems that God made all things at once. For, they say, if He made by His word, why is it not said that He made everything at once? For it is the custom among men to believe that things are made in stages. For the power of God it seems more fitting if it is said that He made all things in one day. However, we see great providence in this work and order. For He could certainly have made all things together; but diverse reason forbade it, and with all these matters set apart, faith must be given to divine Scripture, which says, and often says, For in six days, it says, the Lord your God made heaven and earth, the sea and all that is in them (Exod. 20:11). First then, they ought to have been made in such a way that they might feel and know that they had been made: for when they did not all see themselves at once, but one today, another tomorrow, they recognized that they are contained in a beginning, and in no way could they suspect eternity, since they recognize each other in parts. For if all things had existed at once, there would be no sense of weakness for them, but they would think that they had not begun. For those things which suddenly exist all together by the word of God do not feel themselves being made, unless they see something before themselves and something after themselves. And lest that which was made first might think itself unmade, by seeing greater things made after itself, it believes of itself what it has seen in the other that is nobler. Finally, the light which is called day has before itself heaven and earth, that is, water and dry land. But when water itself and dry land and the confused darkness had been made, they could not claim eternity for themselves, because none of these dared to claim for itself fixedness and identity. Again, the sun and moon, though they are most bright, have many things before them. Therefore it was brought about that the greater things are later, and the earlier lesser things, when they see each other, none of these claims eternity for itself. Furthermore, the work completed in six days contains within itself the whole age of the world, so that the works of six days have the figure of six thousand years: because what in each age was going to happen is contained in order in the works of the six days; for instance, because in the earlier ages there was not going to be such great knowledge of God upon the earth, the earlier days appear without splendor; and that cattle were made before man, because our forefathers, uncultivated and rural, were going to live in the manner of cattle; but that man should be made on the sixth day, this event was brought about because in the sixth millennium of years the coming of Christ made man so that he should not be subject to death. And that man should be the image of God, because by God’s gift he would be conformed in image to the Son of God, as the apostle John says, We know, he says, that when He shall appear, we shall be like Him (1 Jn. 3:2). And the Vessel of election: being conformed, he says, to the image of the Son of God (Rom. 8:29). Moreover, the tree of life which was set in paradise was the image of God’s future grace, which is the body of the Lord; whoever eats it will live forever. For the tree of the knowledge of good and evil signifies that the Law was given through Moses, which, when it made sin known that previously lay hidden, gave the knowledge of good and evil. For it showed what was good and what was evil. And as to the fact that on the seventh day He rested from His works, this signifies that, once the sixth millennium of years is completed, in the seventh millennium He will rest, with the world ceasing from all secular work. We have said these few things out of many, so that we might open a path for understanding according to what we have shown above.

(Genesis 1:1)

1ST CATEGORY OT

QUESTION 2. WHY DID GOD CREATE THE WORLD? — He made it because He is a craftsman; or else it must be denied that He is, if He did not. But His very works show that He exists. He therefore made what previously did not exist, because without doubt it is better to be than not to be. If it is said, “Was there some empty place where He could make it, or what was there before He made it?” The Vessel of Election resolves this briefly. For when speaking of God he says, “In Him we live and move and have our being” (Acts 17:28); that is, all things are in God, because He is everywhere, and before all things He alone is eternal, invisible to every creature. And lest we seem to have passed over the mystery, or rather to have been ignorant why the world was made, we say that the apostasy of the Devil drew many angels, that is, spiritual powers, with him into transgression, when he willed by wicked presumption to defend a kingdom for himself. This the prophet Isaiah signifies, saying, “How are you fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, who used to rise in the morning?” (Isa. 14:12); that is, you who appeared brighter than the rest. For he was a sort of prince of many, among whom he was more splendid, and with whose company he descended into wicked conflict. Seeing beneath himself many spiritual powers, since in the paradise of God he was more excellent in the knowledge of the heavenly mystery, swollen with pride itself, he wished to be called god. In this, moreover, we see in the present life that some have imitated his example: men who, puffed up by the contemplation of the troops of soldiers gathered around them, and with their attendants supplying fuel for conspiracy in this matter, have tried to claim dominion for themselves. From this it came about that God, in order to destroy his presumption not by power but by reason, created matter which would be a confusion of things, from which He would make the world. For the things that were together in confusion, once distinguished, yielded this adornment which we see. When the substances were separated from one another, and a structure made, it is called “world”; because each thing, set apart from another, appeared in the world: so that man, placed here, created from what is above and what is below, that is, from heavenly and earthly elements, might show by the dominion of the one God, not only by voice but also by the image in which one man was made by the one God, from whom the rest would arise, that all things are from one. For One made one, so that He might teach that all are from one, and that therefore God is one; so that the higher creature might learn in man, to its own confusion, truth, he who was formed from the earth. From this the Devil became man’s enemy. For he foresaw that man was made to be his accuser; and so by his subtlety he worked to bring man into the same transgression into which he himself fell, so that he might make his accuser a sharer in his own condemnation. For in the transgression he promised man divinity, from which he himself, when he aimed to it, was cast down. And since every nature is free from guilt, it takes its names from what happens from it. First come things, afterwards their designation; and so “Satan” and “Devil” are names formed from his deeds, so that they signify not his nature but his will. Therefore, so that the purpose of God, which He decreed in the case of created man, should stand firm, and so that the deed of the Devil, by which he deceived man, might increase the weight of his own guilt, Christ agreed to come down from the holy seats even to earth: so that He might free man from the sentence of transgression, and might show the future perdition of the Devil, lest anyone imitate his deed. For this reason the apostle John said, “For this the Son of God came, that He might destroy the works of the Devil” (1 Jn. 3:8). If he were evil by nature, then to promise him punishment would be madness or injustice. For who reproves one whom he sees do nothing except what his nature allows? Can fire be blamed because it burns, or water because it cools, when it does this not by will but by nature? Therefore if the Devil was evil by nature, he would have no will. Nor could he discern; instead, in one and the same way he would rush upon all, like a blind creature. But in fact he acts with a kind of judgment: he spares those who do his will, conceals toward certain beginners, sets obstacles and hindrances before those who seek to flee to God’s help, lays snares for the servants of God, and is more hostile to those who are more zealous in His service. From this it is clear that his will lies in crime. Therefore the apostle Peter says, “Be sober and watchful, because your adversary the Devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking whom he may devour” (1 Pet. 5:8). He does not seek the Gentiles, he does not seek the Jews, he does not seek those of evil life and conduct; he seeks the servants of God and the followers of Christ, whom he knows to be his enemies, because they condemn his deed and his presumption. Indeed, once the Law was given, envy burned more fiercely against those who were under the Law, knowing that the teachings of the Law proclaim one God and good conduct for men. Therefore, if he is thought to do this by nature, he cannot be held guilty: because he does what belongs to his nature and what he can do, and does not do what he cannot do, because it does not belong to his nature. Therefore he is neither to be praised nor condemned. He is not to be praised, because what he does harms; but he is not to be condemned, because he does these things not by will but by the force of nature. For we know that some have suddenly gone mad, and with clubs, iron, stones, and bites have injured many, even killed some; yet when they were captured by skill and brought before judges, they were not held guilty, because they had done these things not by will, but driven by some unknown force, not knowing what they did. For how can he be made guilty who does not know what he has done? So also if the Devil does not know good, why is he judged condemnable for not doing what he does not know? Rather, if it could be so, he would deserve praise because he does what he does not know. We, however, are rightly made guilty, because we do not do what we know we ought to do, or because we do what we know we ought not to do. But since we see throughout all of Scripture that the Devil is presented as guilty, and therefore we read that Hell has been prepared for him, that he is to be condemned by the law, we know this: because when he knew and was able to do good, he did evil. For God, who is just, would not condemn him for not doing the good which he did not know; but because he did the evil which he did know. Therefore I think it is clear that no nature ought to be called evil, because every evil, as has been made evident, arises from the will, which through the senses befalls nature.

(Genesis 1:1)

1ST CATEGORY OT

QUESTION 28. WHAT CAN WE SAY TO THOSE WHO CLAIM THAT THIS WORLD EXISTS NATURALLY FROM ALL ETERNITY, AND THAT IT HAS NEITHER BEGINNING NOR END? — That the world has existed from eternity and is subject to no authority is unlikely and impossible. We see it made up of bodies in such great diversity; yet nothing divine and eternal can be anything but simple, in which no diversity is seen, but only unity. For the world does not even preserve the regular cycles of the seasons, so that it is not only changeable in time or composed of contrary substances, but even in those very cycles of time; whereas what is eternal shuns all diversity and cannot be grasped by touch or sight, being incorporeal. This world, however, is subject to suffering, since water resists fire, and fire, if it grows stronger, overcomes water; and the earth, being by nature dry and cold, suffers burning, as a corporeal thing. Therefore it is inappropriate to call the world eternal, since we see it subject to suffering and failing through age as the ages go by, and we believe that it will come to an end. What is to be thought of the person who believes the world is eternal? Certainly man began in the world: without man, for whom did the yearly fruitfulness of the world profit? Or did it generate without any providence? And how did what is eternal generate corruptible and mortal things, when from what is eternal only what is eternal ought to arise? And that which is visible, felt, and touched, by what boldness is it called eternal? And that which is dispensed in the cycles of time, so that even time itself sometimes does not perform its proper functions, how is it called eternal? For eternity is neither corrupted nor changed.

1ST CATEGORY OT

QUESTION 3. WHAT NEED WAS THERE FOR MOSES TO EXPLAIN LATER, AND NOT EARLIER, THE BEGINNING OF THE WORLD AND THE ORDER OF CREATION? — It was not fitting that it should be described before, because for this reason so great an error did not yet exist among humans. But when error had already grown in the human race, so that even the sons of Israel in Egypt heard from the philosophers of the Egyptians a teaching contrary to this account, those same Egyptians from whom Moses had also learned all Egyptian knowledge, that a certain Apis had fashioned this world through evil angels, and that this one too seems to be the prince of the world, that is, Satan, this view Marcion followed and rushed into death. For the Manichaeans also say that man was made by this same Satan, not this world, being more foolish than the others. For since it is agreed that the world was made for the sake of man, they say that the world was made by God, though from foreign substance; but that man was created by the adversary, as though in another’s house another master were set. It was therefore necessary that Moses, in order to expose and remove this error, should make it clear that God is the author of the world and of man who was made. Having received authority through the signs and wonders that he performed, he taught that what he transmitted with attesting signs was without doubt true. For who would not believe him whose deeds produced such great signs? Therefore it is that those who think contrary to this teaching are known to err, because they strive to support their assertion with bare words. Therefore, in order to teach that nothing is coeternal with God, he sets forth the very order of created things, so that while he mentions that the lesser things were made first, and afterwards the greater, none of these may be thought uncreated: for those that are later in time are greater in power; so that if the former think they have superiority by reason of time, they are refuted by the very weakness by which they are subjected to the latter; or if the latter, presuming on their power, claim primacy for themselves, they are humbled by their posteriority, so that none of these may appear not to have been subject from the beginning. First indeed heaven and earth were made; then light, which serves for day; after that the firmament, which was called heaven, and the gatherings of the waters, which he called seas, so that the earth might appear in which it could be possible to live. By “earth,” which he says was made after heaven, he does not wish us to understand earth alone, but he signified matter, that is, all the lower things which brought forth the whole appearance of the world. “Heaven,” however, he maintains to be not this bodily one, but that higher one which is spiritual, made in the beginning; so that when he says that heaven was first made, then earth, he meant that in heaven all things invisible, and on earth all things visible, were created by God. For he includes the highest and the lowest of the whole of nature, so that whatever lies between is without doubt also believed to have been made. The luminaries moreover, which he appointed for the governance of the world, he declares were made on the fourth day, so that the greater they are in power, the later they are in time. But man he established on the sixth day, so that he might introduce an inhabitant into a house already prepared. And man is far more exalted, who indeed is declared to have been made on the sixth day; whom I therefore called more exalted because his inner nature is invisible and capable of understanding. Yet in strength the sun is greater, and in light the moon is more excellent than the earth. Therefore it is that some are displeased by the statement, “And he saw the light, that it was good”: for since all things were said by them to have been made by evil, they could not be believed to be good. Moses, in order to prove that the things which were made are good, shows that what he made was pleasing to God himself, so that whoever was displeased by them might be shown guilty. For how could he be ignorant of the light, who said, “Let there be light,” and there was light? Or who makes what he does not know? The light that was made pleased him who made it. What craftsman does not rejoice in his work? Therefore it is said, “God saw the light, that it was good” (Gen. 1:3–4). And there is no lack of those who say that it is evil. What, if it had been left without testimony? Therefore, after the structure of the world had been described, the line of the race was carried through from the origin of the first man by Seth, who was given in place of Abel, and in due order it comes down to Abraham, the father of the Jews: so that it might be shown that Abraham believed in this God, who is the maker of the world, and that he himself gave the Law, in which the Christ who was to come was promised, who would free the human race from the dominion of the Devil. From these things our faith is proved reasonable. For the described genealogy bears witness to this, because from the beginning there has been a race of Christians. For from Seth, the son of Adam, one comes to Enoch, from Enoch to Noah, from Noah to Abraham, from Abraham one descends to David, from David to Mary, from Mary Christ is born of the Holy Spirit. Therefore, all those in former times, as many as had faith in the one God whom the Savior proclaimed, are rightly to be called Christians. For from the beginning the coming Savior was promised. Therefore John in the Apocalypse says, “The Lamb who was slain from the foundation of the world” (Rev. 13:8). Therefore there have always been Christians. For all those, whom I mentioned above, from the first man created in the world, through whom the line reaches to the Savior, had faith in this God, of whom Christ spoke when he said: “Now this is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (Jn. 17:3). It may be said by way of objection: If even those earlier people were Christians, what new knowledge came through Christ? The coming of Christ brought this advance in understanding: that the preaching of the one God revealed the mystery, showed what belongs to each person (of the Trinity), and, to the fulfilling of the righteousness of the Law, added what had been reserved.

1ST CATEGORY OT

2ND CATEGORY OT

(Gen. 1:2)

QUESTION 41. AND IS THE SPIRIT WHO WAS MOVING OVER THE WATERS TO BE UNDERSTOOD AS THE HOLY SPIRIT, BECAUSE IT IS SAID, “THE SPIRIT OF GOD WAS MOVING OVER THE WATERS” (Gen. 1:2)?" —   If it seems that he erred in this opinion, what he said must not be accepted. Therefore, by some the Holy Spirit is thought to be meant, because it is read that he is the Spirit of God. But this is a weak and empty assertion: for not only does the order not allow it, and reason refuse it, but the very words themselves are shown to be feeble for establishing this claim. For in the Law we frequently find by these words another meaning indicated. Among other things the Lord God says, “My spirit shall not remain in these men, because they are flesh.” And further on: “But I will wipe out,” he says, “everything from man to beast” (Gen. 6:3, 7). Because he was going to bring a flood upon the earth, can the Holy Spirit possibly be understood here? Did he not speak of souls? For not only are our souls called spirits, but also those of cattle. For it is written therefore: “And all flesh died that moved upon the earth … all in whose nostrils was the spirit of life” (Gen. 7:22). And in the prophet Ezekiel it is said therefore, when God, promising the restoration of men, says, “Therefore says the Lord God to these bones: I will stretch skin over you, and I will put my spirit within you, and you shall live” (Ezek. 37:5). Did he speak of the Holy Spirit and not of the soul? All heavenly beings are indeed spirits, but they differ from one another; and God is spirit (Jn. 4:24; 2 Cor. 3:17), but in a far different way. Therefore, every spirit is of God; yet it is not God, unless it is the spirit which is from him himself. Its distinguishing mark is that it is called holy. For men too are called sons of God, and Christ is called the Son of God; but there is a distance between them, because he is the true Son, they adopted sons. Likewise there is a distinction between “spirit of God” and “Spirit of God.” For the Holy Spirit is from God and consubstantial with him; whereas the other spirits are said to be of God, but they are creatures. Nor is it in accordance with order that the Holy Spirit should be understood as moving over the waters, since reason teaches that over the waters there is a spiritual creature, and that above it there is another superior creature; for one creature differs from another in glory (1 Cor. 15:41): for whatever approaches near to the throne of God has ministries that are more glorious. Therefore the angel Raphael says among other things: “I am,” he says, “one of the seven holy angels who stand and go in before the glory of the Lord” (Tob. 12:15).

(Gen. 1:2)

QUESTION 2. AND IS THE SPIRIT WHO WAS MOVING OVER THE WATERS TO BE UNDERSTOOD AS THE HOLY SPIRIT, BECAUSE IT IS SAID, “THE SPIRIT OF GOD WAS MOVING OVER THE WATERS” (Gen. 1:2)?" — If therefore by some he is thought to be the Holy Spirit because he is read as being the Spirit of God, this is a weak and empty assertion. For not only does order not admit this, and reason reject it, but the very words are found to be feeble for supporting this assertion. By these words something else is often signified in the Law. The Lord God says, “My spirit shall not remain in these men, because they are flesh.” And further on: “But I will wipe out,” he says, “everything from man to beast.” (Gen. 6:3, 7) He says this, of course, because he was going to bring the flood upon the earth. Never here can the Holy Spirit be understood. He spoke of souls. For not only are our souls called spirits, but also those of cattle. For therefore it is written: “And all flesh died that moved upon the earth … all in whose nostrils was the spirit of life.” (Gen. 7:22) And in the prophet Ezekiel it is said therefore, when God, promising the restoration of men, says, “Therefore says the Lord to these bones: I will stretch skin over you, and I will put my spirit within you, and you shall live.” (Ezek. 37:5) Surely the Holy Spirit ought not to be understood merely because it was said by the Lord, “I will put my spirit within you”; since God clearly spoke of the soul. For this is common to every spirit with the Holy Spirit, that in the same way every spirit is called a spirit of God. Understanding is necessary here to distinguish things that share one name. For God is called spirit, and the soul of man is called spirit, and the wind likewise, and the air, and the soul of cattle, and angels, and all that have received to live by their own substance. But by understanding you already distinguish how God is said to be spirit in one way, and the creature in another: just as you understand in one way that Christ is called the Son of God, and in another that men are called sons of God. Whenever Scripture wishes to indicate the spirit that is properly from God, it adds the words “Holy Spirit,” so that by this it may not be understood as a creature, but, because it is from God, it may be believed to be nothing other than God himself. But when Moses was describing the material creation, that is, the confusion of things, which is certainly without rational sense, upon the earth and the deep and the darkness he spoke of the Spirit of God as being moved, so that from that spirit and from the place in which he was moving the higher creature, which we call spiritual, might be known. For even from the fact that he said that he was moving, he indicated that he was a creature, since every creature of God is moving along by the power of him from whom it received to exist. For what order would there be that the Holy Spirit be moving over the waters, when it is certain that he is above all creation? For if Christ is at the right hand of God above all the heavens (Col. 3:1), there also is the Holy Spirit. Things of one and the same dignity and nature must be together: although God is not denied to be everywhere, this is the power of the Trinity, yet the due honor is also preserved, that he is said to be above all creation, so that this is proper to him. Therefore we also say, “Our Father, who are in heaven” (Matt. 6:9); and, “who dwells in unapproachable light” (1 Tim. 6:16).

1ST CATEGORY NT

QUESTION 107. ON THE ORDER OF DAY AND NIGHT. — As far as the structure of the world is concerned, we read of darkness before we read of light. For those things which contributed to the making of the world, and which appear to have been made together, are considered to have been without light; that is, water, earth, darkness, from which the world was compacted, as is contained in Wisdom, which is called Solomon’s, “out of formless matter” (Wis. 11:18), that is, dark matter. For both darkness and water are testified by the sacred books to have been made by the very voice of the Lord through the prophet Isaiah: “I,” he says, “am God, who made the light and created the darkness” (Isa. 45:6–7). Likewise, through David, the Holy Spirit shows both that the waters were made and that the earth was established upon the waters (Ps. 135:6). This agrees both with the authority of the Gospel and the tradition of the Apostles, in which all things are read as having been made; and so that nothing might be excepted, he says, “whether things in heaven or things on earth” (Jn. 1:3; Col. 1:16). Therefore, in this part which pertains to earthly things, we read of darkness before light. This, however, is only in respect to the order of the reading, not in respect to dignity; for of course light is much better than darkness. Yet in the ordering of the world light receives the name by which it is called day, and darkness is called night; but specifically for this reason, that when the darkness is illumined and the light passes, that span of time until the light returns is called night; and that span of time during which the darkness is illumined is called day. When night is named, then, the coming day is expected; and when day is named, the coming night is expected. But when these functions cease, with the passing away of the world, they will be called only darkness and light. For it cannot be called night when there are perpetual shades, nor day when the light has ceased to set. Where eternity is, these names cease, because they began with the world. Indeed, before light was made, which was called day, it is not read that there was night, but darkness; which, after they were illumined and the light passed, were called evening and night. Therefore, as far as appears, night is lesser to day. For just because darkness is mentioned before light, it should not therefore seem to be preferred; since heaven existed before the sun, and yet the sun is greater in brightness; and the earth before man, and cattle and the other animals, and yet they are subject to man. Night therefore must not be set before day merely because darkness is read first; since it is clear that in dignity light precedes darkness, and in time day precedes night. For as was shown above, when there was darkness, light was made. “And God called the light Day, and the darkness he called Night; and there was evening and morning, one day” (Gen. 1:5). For if there had been no day, there would not even be night; there was, in fact, darkness, which, when it was illumined and the day had passed, its course completed, became evening. And when after evening it grew light, the first day came to be, the night having passed, so that night might follow day. This is both fitting and rationally praiseworthy: that a lower nature in all things be subject to a higher. How then is night said to be before day, when you read its name after day? For it would not have been called night, nor evening, unless, once light was made, it had run its course as day; when that ended, evening came to be, which is night. The day indeed became evening, so that you may know that night is a part of day. For the day is completed only when night too has passed. Therefore we say, “The year has three hundred and sixty-five days,” not, of course, without nights. For when we say “days,” we are there including nights as well. Under the authority of “day” we signify night; for if night were the leading term, under the name of night day too would be counted. Who among men says, “After five nights I will see you,” and not, “after five days”? Nor do we remember ever to have read anywhere that night was named before day. For “Moses,” he says, “was on the mountain forty days and forty nights” (Exod. 24:18). And in the Psalm: “The sun,” he says, “shall not burn you by day, nor the moon by night” (Ps. 120:6). And to give an example from the very beginnings: “Let there be,” he says, “luminaries in the firmament of heaven, and let them give light upon the earth: the greater luminary for the beginning of the day, and the lesser luminary for the beginning of the night” (Gen. 1:14). But the moon cannot be set before the sun, just as night cannot be set before day; rather, as the moon is under the sun, so night is under day. And in the Gospel we have both days and nights indicated under the authority and numbering of days. For the Lord says, among other things, “There are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the Son of Man in his kingdom.” And he added, “And it came to pass after eight days” (Luke 9:27, etc.). Are not nights included in this number? And in another place: “These things,” he says, “were done in Bethany beyond the Jordan, where John was baptizing. On the next day he saw Jesus coming.” Did he say, “On the next night”? Again it follows: “On the following day he wished to depart into Galilee” (John 1:28–29, 43). And in what follows: “And on the third day there was a wedding in Cana of Galilee” (Jn. 2:1). See how everywhere day is shown to have authority, having night as its subordinate. For if all were contained under the name of night, night would precede day. Therefore, because the Romans have the rule, the Spaniards and Gauls and Africans and the rest who are subject to them are called Romans under their name; so also night, because it is subject to day, is contained under its name. But some are deceived on this point, because the Jews are ordered to enter the sabbath in the evening, and they do not consider why such a command was given. For indeed they necessarily have to buy food for themselves the day before, and prepare it for the sabbath, and go to wash. Can they do these things by night, so as to enter the sabbath at sunrise? The Lord certainly rose again in the evening, and this is reckoned to the day. For the resurrection is celebrated on a day, which is called the Lord’s Day. Therefore you read, “This is the day which the Lord has made” (Ps. 117:24); yet not “the Lord’s night,” because day holds the primacy For whether on the past day or on the future, night is always placed beneath; because it is lower both in order and in nature, as the Apostle says: You are children of the day and of the light, not of the night nor of darkness (1 Thess. 5:5). And if we judge by the consuls, we shall see that he is named first who is chosen first. Indeed it is customary to say, With him who will be consul? If therefore night were also before day, it would be named first. For the reckoning so truly begins from the day, that, for example, if we say, Tomorrow is the sixth day before the calends, it is of course from morning until another morning is reached, so that a day and a night having passed, the count is complete. For the moon too, of course, was made on the morning of the fourteenth day; for it had to be made to shine for the whole night, and on the next morning the fifteenth began. Why then is there any doubt, that the beginnings are to be taken from the day? On account of the disputes of certain persons about a matter that is obvious, we have been forced to speak at greater length, although the reading itself explains itself, in which day is signified before night with clear reasoning. All these things mentioned above we have said according to the origin of the world. But if we wish to speak more deeply, lifting up our understanding with spiritual strength, we discover it to be unfitting to assert that darkness was created before light. For if the nature of light is heavenly and that of darkness earthly, it is surely senseless to think that light was made after darkness; because Moses says that light was made in that part in which the world now is, not that it was then created; for all spiritual things were created before carnal things, so that the light which was in the heights might come to be in the lower regions, like a lamp in a house. But in what way are darknesses said to be before light, when they are always seen after light? Indeed, heavenly and spiritual things are believed by nature to be light, earthly and carnal things to be darkness; so that the nature of darkness seems to subsist by the power of light, because all that is lowest belongs to what is highest. For if we question, we discover darkness even in the sun itself. For when you are close to it, it appears so very bright that it cannot be looked at; but at a certain distance, still very bright, yet such that it can be seen; but if far away, less bright: the farther, the less bright. From this there appears a certain defect which proclaims darkness, and therefore it comes about that darkness seems to take its rise from light. Therefore he who made light created darkness also in this way, just as in making water he at the same time created earth: so that, as earth is the solid support of water, so darkness is the defect of light. But God alone is he who does not suffer defect, who, although he is everywhere, or rather has all things within himself, is so exceedingly bright that he is seen by no one, unless he is willing to moderate himself. Indeed, although the Savior was in the body and was not shut in, yet he was not seen, unless he willed it. For when he was transfigured on the mountain and appeared in great glory (Matt. 17:1–2), that which, as it were, lay hidden in the body he revealed when he willed. How then was he hidden, who was not enclosed? For if, with his body, he entered to the disciples through closed doors (Jn. 20:19), how does his divinity not penetrate all things? that is, it cannot be shut in, because it does not suffer defect. Since therefore God is absent from nowhere, yet he is said to be there where he appears and wills to be seen. And since all things are in God, because he surpasses all things, as the Apostle says, For in him we live and move and are (Acts 17:28); he himself, nonetheless, is in nothing except in what he wills. By a certain mystery he is in all things, and by a certain providence he appears where he wills.

(Genesis 1:26)

1ST CATEGORY OT

QUESTION 24. WHY, SINCE MAN AND WOMAN ARE ONE FLESH, IS MAN THE IMAGE OF GOD AND NOT WOMAN? — Man and woman are indeed of one substance, both in soul and in flesh; but man holds a higher rank, because woman is from man, as the Apostle says: “The head of the woman is the man” (Eph. 5:25; 1 Cor. 11:3). For it was the cause that made man greater, not the substance. In one body, too, there are greater and lesser members, not by nature, but by arrangement.

(Genesis 1:26) 

1ST CATEGORY OT

QUESTION 45. HOW MAN WAS MADE IN THE IMAGE OF GOD, AND WHETHER THIS WAS FOR DOMINION, AND WHETHER WOMAN TOO? —  “Let us make,” he says, “man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26). Some think this should be understood in light of another passage of Scripture, namely that in which we read that God said, “Come, let us go down and confuse their languages” (Gen. 11:7). For, as far as outward appearance goes, it seems similar: it is one voice speaking in the plural; but it differs in meaning, because the reasons are not the same. There, he speaks of creating man, whom God wills to be created in his image and likeness. But when he says, “Come, let us go down and confuse their languages,” this refers to the fact that men should not understand one another; therefore God can be seen as speaking to the angels, like a commander to his army. He speaks in common, because he was going to act through them, as their Creator; and therefore he says, “Let us confuse their languages.” For when he says, “Let us make man in our image and likeness,” it cannot be said that he spoke to the angels, because one cannot say that there is one single image of God and of the angels, as of an emperor and his companions. For where there is one single image, the dignity and nature cannot be different. Accordingly he added, “And God made man; in the image of God he made him” (Gen. 1:27): so that it is God who said, and God who made; not another or a different god, but the same God. For when one speaks to one, he did not signify a different nature, but a person. For although God is one, there are nonetheless three persons: and therefore there is one God, because whether in the Son or in the Holy Spirit, there is the one substance of God; for what proceeds from that substance cannot fail to be what he himself is. Therefore the person of God the Father is the one who says, “Let us make”; and the person of the Son is the one who makes man in the image of God; whether in the image of the Father or of himself, it makes no difference, because the image of both is one. Moreover, the Son made through the Holy Spirit. For just as the Father is said to make through the Son, so also the Son through the Holy Spirit, since he himself says, “I cast out demons by the Spirit of God” (Matt. 12:28). Therefore one image belongs to the three; because whether Father, Son, or Holy Spirit, there is one God. And consequently man was made one in the image of the one God. Man is the image of God in this respect, that just as there is one God in heaven, from whom all spiritual beings have their existence, so there should be one man on earth, from whom the rest would have their carnal origin. Yet some think that man was made in the image of God with respect to God’s dominion; and because it says, “And let him have dominion over the fish of the sea, and the birds of the air, and all the earth,” whereas not only the man but also the woman is seen to have these things subject to her, though it is certain that she does not have the image of God. This indeed fails in reason on two counts: for in that case it would be asserted that God did not say to the Son, “Let us make man in our image and likeness,” but to the heavenly dominions which the Apostle mentions, if man has the image of God in dominion; and it would be given to the woman, so that she too would be the image of God, which is absurd. For how can it be said of the woman that she is the image of God, when it is certain that she is subject to the rule of the man and has no authority? She can neither teach, nor act as a witness, nor pronounce a legal decision, nor judge; how much less can she exercise command?

1ST CATEGORY OT

2ND CATEGORY OT & NT

(Genesis 1:27)

QUESTION 21. WHAT IT MEANS THAT GOD MADE MAN IN THE IMAGE AND LIKENESS OF GOD, AND WHETHER WOMAN IS THE IMAGE OF GOD? — This is what it means that man was made in the image of God: because the One made one, so that just as all things are from the one God, so also the whole human race is from one man. But the likeness is this: that just as the Son is from the Father, so also the woman is from the man, so that the authority of a single principle may be preserved. Yet the Son was born from God the Father inexpressibly and incomprehensibly; whereas the woman, bodily, as we read (Gen. 2:21–22), was made from the man, so that through her birth might arise. But the Son of God was born for this reason, that through him creation might come into being. In this, therefore, there is a difference. For God was born of God, but a woman from a man: because there, there is simplicity, and it was not possible for the simple to be born except from the simple—spirit from spirit, God from God. Therefore the man is the image of God. For therefore it is written: God made man; in the image of God he made him. Therefore the Apostle also says: “A man indeed ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God; but the woman,” he says, “should cover her head” (1 Cor. 11:7, 6). Why? Because she is not the image of God. Therefore again the Apostle says: “I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man” (1 Tim. 2:12).

(Genesis 1:27)

QUESTION 1. WHAT IT IS TO HAVE MADE MAN IN THE IMAGE AND LIKENESS OF GOD; AND WHETHER WOMAN IS THE IMAGE OF GOD. — Man was made in the image of God in the sense that the one and only God made one man, etc.

 (Genesis 1:31, 7:2)

1ST CATEGORY OT

QUESTION 9. IF ALL THE CREATURES THAT GOD MADE WERE GOOD AND VERY GOOD, WHY DID HE SAY TO NOAH, "BRING WITH YOU INTO THE ARK OF PURE AND UNCLEAN ANIMALS, SINCE NO ONE CAN CALL GOOD WHAT IS UNCLEAN?” (GEN. 1:31; 7:2) — It is because words have many different senses that they give rise to questions. For if they are referred to the specific issue being discussed, there will be no question, since things themselves unfold in due order. Sometimes we call “common” what is undivided; sometimes what is unclean. For “common” is used in two ways. Therefore the Apostle Peter says, “Nothing common or unclean has ever entered my mouth” (Acts 10:14). And the Apostle Paul says, “Everything that does not proceed from faith is sin” (Rom. 14:23); and elsewhere, “The law is not of faith” (Gal. 3:12), and yet it is not sin. You see, then, that one and the same word does not always signify the same thing. So also when something is called “unclean,” we must consider for what reason it is so called: sometimes it is called unclean in comparison with something better; sometimes it is referred to dishonorable deeds, so that it is understood as evil. No substance, therefore, is evil; for those things which are called unclean by reason of their substance are unclean only in comparison with things of surpassing beauty. For a dog is called unclean compared with a sheep; lead is unclean compared with gold; a raven compared with a peacock. And though they are all members of one body, some are called honorable and others dishonorable, even though they are known not to be evil. Therefore all things are good in their own nature, because they are useful. 

(Genesis 2:7)

1ST CATEGORY OT

QUESTION 23. CAN SOULS, THEN, BE TRANSLATED JUST LIKE BODIES? — I think it is dishonorable to say that souls are generated together with bodies, so that a soul is born from a soul, a thing that does not belong even to the soul itself. Or if indeed each of the heavenly powers was made individually, and from them the rest came to be, then it might seem believable that from the one soul of Adam the other souls are born. But this is not fitting, because this was possible for God alone, that the simple should generate, and was not granted to others. This is so mysterious in the case of the Savior that it is considered unbelievable not only by pagans or Jews alone, but even by those who call themselves Christians. For the Photinians and Arians reject this faith and do not believe that God has generated. For if at the time when the body is sown the soul also is generated from a soul, we read that a rib was taken from Adam, yet we do not read that a soul was born from a soul. But if the rib had a soul with it, then it was not born, but removed as a part. Yet this too is not written. The prophet Zechariah says among other things: “Who formed the spirit of man within him” (Zech. 12:1). Nor does Isaiah disagree with this, for he says: “Therefore says the Lord God who made you and formed you in the womb” (Isa. 44:2). If therefore it is formed in the womb, then it is given to an already shaped body. For when it fills all the members of the body, it is said to be fashioned in the body. Just as water, although without form, when poured into a vessel appears to be shaped, so the soul, though by nature incorporeal and simple, is as it were formed in the body, giving life to each of the members. Moses has handed this down more clearly, saying: “If someone strikes a woman who is pregnant in the womb, and she miscarries: if what is in her is fully formed, let him give soul for soul; but if it is unformed, let him be fined” (Exod. 21:22), so that he might prove that the soul is not present before the form. Therefore, if it is given to a body already formed, it is not born at the conception of the body, derived with the seed. For if the soul exists with the seed and comes from another soul, many souls perish every day, since the seed by a certain outflow does not come to birth. But if we look more closely, we shall see what we ought to follow. Let us consider the making of Adam. In Adam an example was given, so that from him it might be understood that a soul was received by an already formed body. For God could have mixed the soul with the clay of the earth and so have formed the body. But he proceeded with reason, because the house had first to be put together and then the inhabitant brought in. The soul, certainly, since it is spirit, cannot dwell in dryness; therefore it is carried in the blood. Consequently, when the features of the body have not yet been put together, where will the soul be? Does it wander outside until it is put in, although reason teaches that it is given in such a way as to animate the body, not to wander idly? But from whom is it given, let those who think otherwise tell us: from the male, or from the female? If from the female, it is not fitting, because the example is otherwise. For they propose that with the rib taken from the man, a soul was also given; and we have shown by many arguments that this is invalid. From this it might perhaps seem to be given from the female, especially on account of the Savior, whom we know to have been born of a woman from the Holy Spirit, without the union of flesh. But if they suppose this, they give more to women; for they transfer the authority of the man to the woman. Since they claim that the origin of both body and soul is from the man, they turn around and say that what is more important, namely the soul, is from the woman, and what is less, namely the body, is from the male; although it is clear that the order of the example given by God cannot be altered.

(Genesis 2:7)

1ST CATEGORY NT

QUESTION 123. DID ADAM HAVE THE HOLY SPIRIT? — I have found that some of our brethren have not fully examined the Scriptures, but in simplicity of mind affirm that when Adam was made, he received the Holy Spirit, which he lost when he sinned, just as it is now given to believers. Led by this reasoning, by which many are accustomed to assert that through faith man is restored so that, being brought back to his former state, he receives all that Adam had obtained in the beginning; and because he is said to be made a perfect man, they say that if he did not have the Holy Spirit, he was imperfect. But I say that not only man, but also all things which God made, which cannot be said to have received the Holy Spirit, are perfect. For all kinds of animals are perfect in their own nature, so that they may accomplish that for which they are made: so also man is perfect in his own kind, so that he is able to discern evil from good, crooked from straight. For he is an intelligible creature, perfect for that for which he was made. He is capable of speaking, planning, and acting, so that what he cannot accomplish by strength, he fulfills by understanding. And how have they dared to say that man ought to be born perfect and to know everything, when they see that he knows nothing beyond what he learns here? For what he does not learn here, he does not know. Finally, since he does not learn here what he is like, he does not know: therefore, since he does not know what he is like, how does he know all things, when knowing oneself is less than knowing other things? But because he learns about other things, and does not learn about himself, he knows about others, but does not know about himself, neither what he is like, nor whether he exists before the body or after the body. For if he had been made so perfect that he needed nothing, he would not have been man, but God; nor would he, being deceived, have transgressed. But to have the Holy Spirit is beyond the nature and perfection of man, so that he may be able to do the things that are of God. Was it not beyond its perfection that the donkey spoke to Balaam (Num. 22:28)? For it received so that it might do what was not of its own nature, but of ours. Therefore, since man is superior to the other animals, must those be said to be imperfect? Or because the holy angels are not what God is, are they imperfect? Or because the luminaries and stars are inferior to the heavenly angels, or because the clouds with their veil obscure the sun and the moon, are they less perfect? And because the members need one another (for the feet cannot do what the hands can), shall they be called imperfect? Far from it. For all things are firm and perfect in their own places and ranks, so that they fulfill that for which they are made. Therefore all things are perfect, because their Creator is also perfect; but in comparison with him they are imperfect. For God is perfect in all things, as the fountain and origin of all. Now the things that have been made are indeed perfect, but with regard to that for which they were made, so that in another respect they are not perfect; because one needs another: so that in that respect in which it does not need, it is perfect, not in that in which it needs: and therefore all things are both perfect and imperfect. Hands need feet; for unless the feet walk, the hands will be idle. Again, the feet need hands; for they cannot shoe themselves nor care for themselves. Therefore, although the body is perfect with its members, it nevertheless cannot fly, nor bear as much as a mule can. And although these (animals) are perfect, they still do not know how to govern themselves, nor can they apply medicine to themselves. Where it is said, Do not be like horse and mule, which have no understanding (Ps. 32:9). And water and fire, though they oppose one another, are perfect in their own kind; for they fulfill that for which they were made. Fire cooks and consumes; it purifies and heats: water, however, washes, cools, irrigates, and refreshes the thirsty. Therefore, since all things are perfect in their own kind, yet without man they can do nothing, nor can man, although he is more perfect, do anything without them. Therefore the Apostle calls us imperfect and perfect. For in comparison with unbelievers we are perfect, because we know God: but because we know less than we ought of the things that are promised, since in this life we cannot comprehend as much as that which is believed, we are imperfect. Therefore, since they think that Adam’s perfection is restored to believers, let us see whether this restoration has anything beyond the divine gift which Adam had obtained. For when Adam was made, he was placed in paradise that he might work there and keep it: that is, that he might cultivate the land and keep the commandments of God, by which he might know that he had received dominion over all things in such a way that he himself should nevertheless live under the law of the Creator, lest his dominion should exalt him, and, puffed up with pride, he should become forgetful of his Maker. He was therefore placed there so that his life might be sustained by food: but through Christ this has been granted, that those who rise again do not need food or drink; because what is mortal in man is transformed into life. Adam was made to dwell on earth; but faith has consented to grant that our dwelling be in heaven. Scripture itself bears witness, for it says, The first man Adam was made a living soul, but the second man a quickening spirit. The first man was of the earth, earthly; the second man was from heaven, heavenly. As is the earthly, such also are the earthly; and as is the heavenly, such also are the heavenly (1 Cor. 15:45–48). What is clearer than that Adam did not have the Holy Spirit? For he was made a living soul; but through Christ (we are made) a quickening spirit, so that man may in some way be similar to the Creator whom he believes. For since the mystery of faith, which is given for salvation, is threefold, he becomes threefold, in body, soul, and Holy Spirit, through whom we are called sons of God: a title which Adam is by no means proved to have received; for he was made earthly. But the sons of God, born not carnally but spiritually, are said to be heavenly. Behold, the gift of God has clearly granted much more grace to man in the time of the Savior than Adam had received; for he has not only been restored, but also improved: restored in that he has been washed from sins; improved in all other respects. For both justice and reason demanded that God’s mercy in granting benefits should be more abundant at the time when He willed the mystery of His divinity to become known to His creature: so that, coming to know what had been unknown for ages and generations, that the mystery of the one God subsists in the Trinity, those cleansed from sins, as though by a kind of dedication to this novelty itself, might furthermore be justified, and, adopted by God, receive the Holy Spirit, by whom they appear to bear the mark of adoption. For adoption from God ought to bear the sign of God the Father, so that they are rightly called sons of God. This gift too was promised through the Prophets, to be given at the time when the mystery of God was to be revealed in the triumph of conquered death, so that the creature might know that the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit are one God. Therefore the Evangelist says: “The Spirit was not yet given, because Jesus was not yet glorified” (Jn. 7:39). For this is glorification: when, by His power, He is recognized as being what He testified about Himself; because this glorification bestowed that gift which had been promised through the prophet Joel. For God says: “In the last days I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh, etc.” (Joel 2:28).
