And the Apostle says among other things: “But when the kindness and love for man of God our Savior appeared; not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to His mercy He saved us, by the washing of regeneration and renewal in the Holy Spirit, which He poured out upon us richly through Jesus Christ our Savior, so that, having been justified by His grace, we might become heirs according to the hope of eternal life” (Titus 3:4–7). The Apostle confirmed what had been promised through the prophet Joel, because after Jesus was glorified God fulfilled this: that He should pour out the Holy Spirit upon those who believe in Christ. And this is to become an heir of eternal life: to receive the Holy Spirit; so that, because the Spirit is eternal, the one who receives Him should have eternal life: for He is the pledge of immortality. Whoever receives Him and abides in His love, when this life is passed, goes on to heaven to Him whose Spirit he possesses. For it would be strange that one who departs therefore having the Holy Spirit should be held in the lower regions. The Spirit of Christ is in man as a mark of Christ’s victory by which He conquered death, so that whoever has His Spirit cannot be held in Hades. And therefore in the ancient saints the Holy Spirit was not present in the same way as He is now in the faithful; for when they departed from this world, they were in the underworld: and it cannot be said that the Holy Spirit, because of Adam’s sin, which through the transmission of the race made all his offspring subject to the underworld, was held under the same sentence that was given to Adam. Therefore, that the Holy Spirit was with the Prophets and righteous men is not doubtful: with the Prophets, on account of the dispensation; with the righteous, on account of holiness, as is read of holy Simeon, because, it says, “the Holy Spirit was upon him” (Luke 2:25); not as a mark of adoption in him, but by reason of his merits. For sons of God who believe only began to exist when the Son of God was revealed, death conquered, to the whole creation. But if it is said that the Holy Spirit was in Adam or in others in the same manner as He is now in the faithful, what new gifts did God bestow when He dedicated in us the kingdom of His Son? And how can the time of the Savior’s coming be called happy and blessed above others if He bestowed the same things that had already been bestowed? And where is that saying in which the Savior says to His disciples: “Many Prophets and righteous men have desired to see what you see, and to hear what you hear, and have not heard” (Matt. 13:17)? By what reasoning, then, can it be said that the blessedness of this time has brought no greater gift than was granted to the ancients? This indeed turns to the dishonor of the Savior, as though He had nothing new to give to those who received Him at the rise of His kingdom; although the wealthy are accustomed to labor so that on the festive day of their birthday they may offer rare gifts to their invited guests. How great, then, is the injustice, that God, being said to have invited people to a new and unheard-of festival day, worthy of all praise, should be thought to have had no unprecedented gifts to bestow? And where is that statement of the Evangelist John, who says: “He came unto His own, and His own did not receive Him; but as many as received Him, He gave them power to become sons of God, to those who believe in His name, who were born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God” (Jn. 1:11–13)? How, then, is it not something unheard-of that God bestowed upon believers in Christ, when He gave them the power to become sons of God, that is, brothers of His own Son, not by the will of the flesh or of man, but of God, so that they might be born spiritually? Or if it is proved that this grace had previously been granted, then it must be said that the coming of Christ brought nothing new. Adam’s making, surely, was carnal and earthly, not spiritual. For he was not born of God without flesh and blood, but made by God from earth: and therefore he could not receive the Holy Spirit, since he was not spiritual, and it had not been granted to him to call God “Father” in prayer. Those who receive the Holy Spirit are given the power that, by reason of having the Holy Spirit, they may call that One the Father of Christians in prayer. Because this had not previously been granted, the ancients cannot be said to have had the Holy Spirit. Those therefore who think that Adam or others had the Holy Spirit do not understand what kind of gift they have from God; nor can they give fitting thanks to Him, since, though receiving more than the others, they say that they have obtained nothing beyond what the others received.

(Genesis 2:7)

2ND CATEGORY OT

QUESTION 3. WHEN ADAM WAS MADE BY GOD AND GIVEN LIFE, HE RECEIVED THE HOLY SPIRIT; FOR IT IS WRITTEN, “GOD BREATHED INTO HIS FACE THE SPIRIT OF LIFE” (Gen. 2:7). — It was not fitting that he should receive the Holy Spirit then; for this was reserved by God for the future, so that in the last days, when the mystery of the one God was revealed, it would be given to believers. From the beginning the Trinity was indeed preached, but the understanding of it was, as it were, under a veil. For the person of God the Father was first preached and revealed without delay and without figure, because all things are from him. But the persons of his Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, and of the Holy Spirit were not kept silent, yet they were not revealed. Accordingly, there arises a question from the faithless concerning the Lord, and concerning the Holy Spirit. For certain madmen say that the Holy Spirit is himself the Father, just as Sabellius says that the Father is the same as the Son. But no one doubts about the person of God the Father. When therefore the revealing of the Trinity takes place, then at last the Holy Spirit is given to believers, so that his person may be revealed, and those who receive him may have the sign that they are children of God, in that they have within themselves the Spirit of God, who is of course from God. For this is the indication of perfection: when it is known that there is both Father and Son and Holy Spirit. This perfection grants this gift. For when the Son of God comes, opening and revealing these things, he must give something more, and it is fitting that he bestow this perfection on believers; for neither in the Son alone, nor in the Father alone is there perfection or salvation, but in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Therefore John the Evangelist says that from his fullness we have all received, grace for grace; “for the Law was given through Moses, but grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (Jn. 1:16–17). It is clear that when the Savior comes, the fullness of truth is brought about. For the things that were hidden, and that which was promised, when it is revealed and made clear, the fullness of truth comes to be; then, when believers receive the Holy Spirit, they become children of God. For the “breathing” which is said to have been done by God into Adam is the imparting of the soul; for “spirit” is frequently used in place of “soul,” as the Gospel says among other things: “And,” it says, “his spirit returned to her” (Luke 8:55). And in the Psalm: “A contrite spirit and a humbled heart God will not despise” (Ps. 50:19). Yet frequently some manuscripts do not read “God breathed,” but “God blew into his face the breath of life, and man became a living soul.” Not because it says “breath of life” did it thereby signify the Holy Spirit. For it says the same of animals: “In which was the breath of life” (Gen. 7:22). It is called “breath of life” because it animates bodies unto life.

(Gen. 2:15-17) 

2ND CATEGORY OT

QUESTION 4. WHY DID GOD IMPOSE UPON ADAM THAT HE HAD PLACED IN THE WORLD A COMMANDMENT, A LAW, AFTER HAVING GIVEN HIM DOMINION OVER ALL CREATURES? — Although Adam was placed in the world and received a command or law, while he himself held dominion over the rest, yet, though Adam was set as lord in the world, because he did not receive this from himself but from God, he had to receive the meaning of this reality from the law; so that he who appears to be lord might, through the law, be subject to the One who had given him this power; so that the authority of the Creator, through the law, might inspire reverence in him, lest so great a dominion exalt him and cause him to become forgetful of God, his Maker.

(Genesis 3) 

QUESTION 127. THE SIN OF ADAM AND EVE. — I consider it beyond doubt that this world was fashioned for the sake of man: which, although composed of diverse substances, is yet one body fitted with many members, so that from these, through their mutual workings, those things might arise which were to be necessary for man. For a dwelling was made for man together with necessities, in such a way that each of these, according to its kind, should be produced upon the earth; that is, that once made, they should possess an inherent power of propagation in each several kind of the things that were created upon the earth. For origins were established, whose seed should advance to the procreation of multiplying kinds upon the earth. Where Scripture bears witness: And God blessed them, saying, Increase and multiply upon the earth (Gen. 1:22, 28). In like manner also the human race was blessed: which meaning we behold in the Law. For we see it written: The people grew and was multiplied in Egypt (Acts 7:17). With the same blessing, therefore, with which the things created for man’s use were blessed, man himself was blessed, that likewise from male and female the stock of the human race should increase and be multiplied upon the earth; and that just as seeds were to be improved by cultivation, so also the human race, by applying care, should endeavor that, once they had attained the knowledge of the Creator, they would restrain their way of life so as to win His favor, that all things together might advance to the praise and glory of the Creator. And since these words signify nothing else, the facts themselves bear witness. For all things that have been made have, by God’s will, been multiplied and improved upon the earth. Nor indeed could it happen otherwise than as God’s will and blessing have decreed for the seeds. How then can it be said that what increases by God’s blessing and with His favor is done evil or is not permitted? The tradition of this matter has remained in the Synagogue and is now celebrated in the Church, namely that God’s creature be joined under God’s blessing. Not at all by presumption, since the pattern has been given by the very Author. But if it is thought that it ought to cease, then it must cease when those things also cease which likewise were blessed that they might multiply: for if the generation of men ceases, to what purpose do those things come into being which were blessed upon the earth? For the world cannot act in part and in part cease. Either it all works, or it all rests in idleness. Is a body useful whose some members are vigorous, others are numb? Why then is that which has been blessed by the Lord asserted by some to be a filthy and contaminated work, unless because a kind of violence is done to the hands of God Himself? For they would not condemn this deed unless they thought ill of God, the Author of this work. Because they fear to detract openly from God, nevertheless they accuse Him through the work He has devised. For when the work displeases, the author is criticized. If men of this sort would read, or rather receive, the Scriptures, they would remember Balaam saying: How shall I curse him whom God has blessed? (Num. 23:8). For it is in vain that he is accused who is praised by the judge; rather, he himself is his own accuser who declares guilty him whom the laws defend. Who then are you who think that that which you read has been blessed by God should be condemned, unless either you deny that this is God, or accuse the Scripture of falsehood? There are those who, as if receiving new things, think that the old must be rejected. But the new precepts, proclaimed to the peoples through Christ, do not differ from these. For He Himself, when invited, did not disdain to go to a wedding; and not only did He honor it with His presence, but also supplied what was lacking for joy (Jn. 2:1–11). For it is written that wine makes glad the heart of man (Ps. 104:15 and Sirach 40:20). And to show that He did this in accordance with the will of God His Father, when the Jews asked whether it is lawful for a man to put away his wife, He answered among other things, saying: For from the beginning God made them male and female, and said: For this cause shall a man leave his father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh. Therefore now they are no more two, but one flesh. What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate (Matt. 19:4–6). Therefore it is that He went willingly when invited to the wedding, lest He should seem to weaken the work of God and of His Father. Rather, showing that the teaching of the old and new Law agrees, He not only did not forbid marriage, but consented to be present at it, bearing witness that God is its Author; and by a saving precept He showed that what has been joined by God ought neither to be forbidden nor separated. And because birth is beneficial, when He was already leaving the world He entrusted His mother to John His disciple (Jn. 19:26–27). Wherefore we also, in all things observing the commands of the old and new Law, are taught to honor our parents (Deut. 5:16 and Matt. 15:4): and it is laid down in the Law that unless we do so, we shall suffer a curse. What then is this presumption, or from what law does it arise, to close off the entrance to marriage, when both the new and the old Law in all respects seem to favor these things? But it is that which we read, that whatever is beyond is from evil (Matt. 5:37). Where the Apostle says that men of this sort have their conscience seared, who forbid to marry and teach abstinence from foods which God created to be received (1 Tim. 4:2–3). For they are shown to do this in hypocrisy, for the sake of hostility, so that they may charge the Law delivered by God. Others, therefore, by striving to resist saving precepts, stretch out opposing hands, that they may praise the orders of crooked doctrine: and therefore they are said to have their conscience seared. For with a corrupt mind, knowing one thing, they profess another. So also the Jews, who, not ignorant that the works done by the Savior were works of the Holy Spirit, out of envy said that He casts out demons by Beelzebub (Matt. 12:24), in order to turn the people away from faith in Him. Such also is the cunning of the above-mentioned people, for in order to pretend that they are lovers of holiness and chastity, they say that marriage must be condemned, so that by this they may win commendation and turn the people away from the truth. And that they may pretend that they study abstinence, they teach that one must refrain from certain foods, so that by this they may show themselves as strangers to the world hastening to the heavenly kingdoms; and by this, after ensnaring the minds of people, they then teach that what is unlawful is permitted, and condemn what is lawful as though it were forbidden. These are the tricks of Satan, that he may invert causes and, as if insinuating something new, shut out the truth, in which there is nothing new, because all is eternal. Who does not see that this way of thinking has been manufactured by adversaries? For who would dare to reject what God has established, and what has never harmed anyone except the enemy of truth? He, in order to cover his own uncleanness, proclaims a holiness which he does not love, so that while he presents himself as if of good will on its account, he may persuade people to unlawful things as if they were lawful. For he recommends himself in order that he may deceive more easily, and by this, when the unwary are taken captive, he suggests things through which he makes them greater sinners: for so that he may apply some supposed remedy to his own cause, he strongly urges people to sin, seeking great comfort from this, in that he shows he has many partners in his crime, reckoning the punishment light, as though it were less grievous if he sees many with him in Gehenna. Blind men, while they are overcome by vices, defend themselves either by weakness or by ignorance, instead of taking vengeance on those things by which a deceiving desire leads them astray. Or what hindering darkness is there, that what is true is not seen? For letters are often thought to signify something else, when either they are not pronounced correctly, or are improperly divided. But when it is read, “God made,” and, “He blessed what He had made,” who can from this argument? who can doubt? who can think that what has been blessed is accursed, unless he is animated by another spirit? If this were said to be the voice of a man, perhaps some deceit might be believed: it is said that God is speaking, and do you doubt? God has blessed, and you reject it? But perhaps, under the name of God, Moses introduced an error? Let the signs and wonders done through Moses in Egypt satisfy you; let the marvels done in the Red Sea for the deliverance of the children of Israel persuade you. Hear the magicians confessing, “This is the finger of God” (Exod. 8:19). Agree with the Apostle when he says, “I would not have you ignorant, brothers, that all our fathers were under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea, and all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:1–4). And from where did the Apostle say this? Scripture is at hand, in which we read our Lord Christ saying to the Jews, “If you believed Moses, you would perhaps believe also in me, for Moses wrote about me” (Jn. 5:46). Who will deny faith to this harmony? Who will dare to say that what is one is at variance? Who is of such a wicked mind as to strive to make undivided love appear as hate? Behold, you have both the testimony of words and examples of virtues, which may subject your mind to the truth, so that you may not think anything else true than what the books of the Catholic Church contain. Since therefore it has been proved that the same God was in the Old Testament who is now ours, and that he is true, as shown by many evidences of his power, his authority must be preferred to such a degree that even what seems harsh and perhaps absurd to us must be accepted and allowed, and thought of otherwise than we imagine, if it is praised by the judgment of God; because we must believe God more than ourselves. For our weakness and lack of skill usually judge as useful what is harmful, and reckon false things as true: which it is wicked even to suspect concerning God. For he is not a nature that can be deceived: how much less, then, should there be doubt concerning marriages, when God says, “What God has joined together, let no man separate”? (Matt. 19:6) For this is a matter clear and simple. Surely every person rejoices when he has been found worthy of God’s favor, and believes himself made better when he learns the mystery of his Creator, which he certainly would not have attained if he had not been born. Why then does he lament what he rejoices in, and condemn that which he boasts of having learned? For if he rejoices because he has learned, but would not have learned unless he had been born, without doubt it is good to be born, because the fruit of birth is the knowledge of the truth. But if it is evil to be born, then knowledge will not be good. For to what purpose will knowledge profit, if birth is condemned? For if it is not useful to be born and it ought not to be, it is useless that one who is to be condemned should learn. But since no one is so dull as to deny that the knowledge of God benefits people, and that it is good and useful, for through it birth itself is made better, so that, when birth is improved, it may merit more than what had been granted to Adam, for believers will reign in heaven, not on earth, in the paradise of God the Father, not in that in which Adam had been commanded bodily to work. For if the feast of the dedication was celebrated at Jerusalem, that is, the festival of the dedication of the temple of God was kept, how much more should the birthday of the human person be celebrated, who is more truly the temple of God; for whose sake also the temple was built by hands, that thanks might be given to God. For our body is a better temple: because it is the work of God, whereas that other was built by human labor; and this is under the hope of eternity, that for destruction. Therefore whoever knows that he was born by God’s appointment, in order that he may give him thanks, having understood his mystery, ought to rejoice on his birthday, seeing that his birth has made progress. Truly, however, those ought not to have been born who, abandoning their Creator, assign his glory to others: for their birth leads on to punishment; but it is not birth that suffers guilt, but the will. But who are you who forbid marriage? Perhaps you are Marcion, because you think the body was not made by God, but by the Devil; while you insist that the soul fell by some error, so that it came to the regions of darkness in which the world now is. How then could he be freed from here, if he were prevented from being generated? For once born you came to know your condition, and with deliberate effort you acted so as to return to your native home, restored to your rightful lot. Indeed, you say you give thanks to Christ, through whom you rejoice that you have attained this understanding. Now consider: if you had not been born, this knowledge would cease, and liberation would not follow. Therefore, if you rejoice that the soul is freed, favor birth; for if you oppose birth, you are an enemy of souls. Or if you are a Manichaean, who reject marriage as though it were something contrary, I ask you: if bodies were not generated at all, how would the soul, which you claim to have been poured into the region of darkness and to be clinging to material things, be rescued from here? For in your books you have written that it is freed by being born, so that souls received from the moon and departing from bodies are handed over to the sun, whom you assert to be the god of your souls. For you are glad to be called Manichaeans. By this very name you demand your liberation: which you certainly would not know of, if you had not been born. Therefore it is very clear that you condemn marriage hypocritically. For while professing holiness, you secretly strive after impurity, something that has been made known not only privately, but also through imperial edicts. Now listen, Catholic, and learn from the Gospel that man’s birth is beneficial. When Simeon, a righteous man, wished to depart from this world, thinking that the knowledge of the Creator without understanding His mystery was sufficient for him, he was not allowed to die unless he advanced further in his perception of God, so that he might have the full reward of his faith. Accordingly, receiving the newborn Savior in his arms, he blessed God and said: “Lord, now you are letting your servant depart, according to your word, in peace; for my eyes have seen your salvation” (Luke 2:29–30). It has been clearly shown that man’s birth is a blessing from God, since to a righteous man thinking of death the answer was given that he would not die before he had seen the Lord’s Christ: for he advanced so far in life that he became worthy, even in the present, to see the One whom he hoped would be his deliverer after death. He, then, who was preserved in life and not allowed to die until he had seen the fruit of his hope, so that he might be assured that he would pass from life to life, how can it be said that birth was of no benefit to him? If it were an evil that we are born, paradise would not be promised, nor eternal life, nor the kingdom of heaven, but punishment and the destruction of hell; so that someone who knew himself to be born for perdition would fear to beget another, and he who knew himself to be unlawfully born would not desire to beget. But perhaps it will be said: The kingdom of heaven is indeed promised, but to the faithful and those who do good. Correct. You see, then, that men do not become guilty because they are born, but because they have lived badly. Nor is the kingdom of heaven promised to those who are not born, so that it might be charged against birth in the case of those to whom it will not be given; rather, it is promised to those who are born and act well, so that birth may neither benefit one who acts badly nor be able to harm one who acts well. For by the faithful and those who act well, birth is improved; but by the faithless and those who act badly, it is made worse. For birth is like a tree that is grafted: if it is grafted with a good shoot, it will become better and be called good; but if it is grafted with a bad shoot, it will become worse and be called not good but evil. So also, if good teaching is joined to birth, it will produce good fruits; but if bad teaching is joined to it, it will produce bad fruits. Therefore, just as a tree is necessary in order that something may be grafted onto it, so birth is necessary in order that there may be something that can make progress. But an objection is raised on the other side: If birth is useful, why are we reborn? We would not be reborn unless birth were useful. To be reborn is to be renewed, and those who are renewed are restored. Therefore rebirth does not accuse birth, but reshapes it; and what is reshaped is thereby shown to have been well established from the beginning. Therefore, in being reborn we are changed in our nature, through the purification of the body, so that we may be restored to Adam’s original condition. It is by the soul’s sin that the body has been stained; when it is repaired and improved through faith, the disposition is washed clean: so that just as it had been defiled through contempt of God, so through obedience it may be cleansed, in order to escape the sentence passed on Adam and be able to rise again. If, then, sin began from the soul, why is the nature of the body blamed, since in Adam’s sin the cause was not bodily desire, but the soul, enticed by hope of divinity, transgressed God’s command so as to subject his body to sin, and men might be born under sin? Yet this in no way harms a man, if he obeys the law of God, except that he dies; and for this very thing God’s goodwill has promised a reward, so that, since in devotion to the Creator they are found faithful, yet through Adam’s transgression they have been subjected to corruption and death, for this reason they may receive from God the Judge more than was granted to Adam: that in the future they may be both glorious and possess eternal life, and be called adopted sons of God; so that it is a gain that they have been born. From this point I will now return to the remaining part of the passage. When man was placed in paradise, he received this command: “From every tree that is in paradise for food, you shall eat. But from the tree by which good and evil are distinguished, you shall not eat from it.” (Gen. 2:16-17) All the trees he mentions are fruits for the nourishment of creatures. Indeed, they are called “trees” by one name, but various fruits are understood. Yet all are trees, and there is one kind of eating, though the things eaten are different. For when God had created many fruit-bearing trees for man to eat, as I said, he forbade eating from one tree; so that those who had received everything in their power might have some reverence for the Creator, in that one tree was reserved, whose use they did not have permission for, so that they would remember the condition of the law. But how was the kind of sin understood from the sentence? For this sentence applies suitably to a murderer, a criminal, an adulterer, and a disgraced man. Achar also, the son of Charmi, when he had sinned, was condemned to be destroyed along with all his household (Joshua 7:1). How then can this sentence be understood as indicating the kind of sin? It can be recognized that it was a great offense, but not understood what kind of offense it was. For we know that others have been condemned by this sentence, though they are known to have sinned in different ways. Both the Amorites and the Sodomites are known to have perished with all their own. Therefore it happens that people guilty of one sin are struck by different sentences, and sinners of different crimes are punished by one and the same kind. Therefore from the sentence given to Adam and Eve the type of their sin cannot be understood. For although their sin was one, yet each, man and woman, received the sentence according to their own person; and likewise the serpent, so that they would not only fail to remain as they had been made, but that labor would also be added to them as punishment. For when all cattle and living creatures had been made subject to man, as we read (Gen. 1:26), the serpent, contrary to this order, raised itself up and by deceit and fraud brought man, once deceived, into subjection to itself. For without doubt whoever captures someone makes that person beneath himself. Therefore, so that the serpent’s cunning would not have its effect, God’s sentence calls it back and brings it down further than it had been made, lest it should be above man, so that by its craftiness it would not only grieve that it had gained nothing, but also that it had become worse. For although it is read to have been more wise than the other beasts, after it deceived man it was made more cursed than all the beasts of the earth. After the sentence given upon the man, the sentence upon the woman, the sentence upon the serpent, it follows that the woman also, whom he had joined to himself for the despising of God’s law, should receive her sentence. He says to her: “Multiplying I will multiply your hardships and your groaning: in sorrow you shall bear children, and to your husband shall be your turning, and he shall rule over you” (Gen. 3:16). No one confirms what he reproves. If children were therefore granted because she had seized intercourse, then the violation has consulted more. But since he said, “In sorrow you shall bear children,” if you think that generation took its beginning from there, where then is what was said, “Increase and multiply”? Understand therefore that this was added only as punishment, so that what had previously been granted with joy should be subjected to sorrow as penalty; and in order that a worse and multiplied punishment should always press upon the woman, the turning to the man is added, so that from this her pain might be renewed again. If the Lord was condemning intercourse, why did he add among the things imposed, “And to your husband shall be your turning”? No one establishes as a punishment what he condemns; for punishment is of course contrary to condemnation, and never arises from the same thing, but from what is opposed to it. If they were in one and the same, no one would fear condemnation. Then someone would award this as a favor, from that very thing in which he saw the law transgressed. This would be to confirm, not to punish, the sin, if for this reason the woman’s turning to the man, and, from that which she practices and not from that which is true, turning, given simply before, were believed to have been imposed upon her as punishment together with a final servitude, because through the woman granted to him the man had been made subject. And without doubt she seemed superior, whose advice he used, thinking that what she urged would benefit him, so that the work of God might appear destroyed by the serpent’s cunning. This is restored by the sentence established by God, so that the woman returns, humbled, to the subjection of her condition under the man, as it had been ordained; and that is added to her which is added as punishment, when she hears, “Multiplying I will multiply your sorrows and your groaning: in sorrow you shall bear children, and to your husband shall be your turning, and he shall rule over you.” Had it been decreed otherwise than that the woman should be subject to the rule of the man? From this, therefore, it is clear that the woman has been called back to what she was, with an addition. Therefore he says, “Multiplying I will multiply your sorrows and your groaning.” What he multiplies, he increases in what already exists, not in what does not exist, it seems he is working. By this sentence, therefore, that had gone before, “Increase and multiply” (Gen. 1:22, 28), the work of creating does not begin, but the ruin of the creature to which it had been granted. To the woman, sorrow is added in bearing children, difficulty is imposed, but no new form of procreation is constructed. For if generation is rightly thought to arise from this, it can rather be understood that generation came from the serpent’s creativity than from the Lord’s; and it is truly, as he said, “Brood of vipers” (Matt. 3:7). But if anyone thinks himself therefore born, let him consider what he deserves, that on account of sin his pain in childbirth might be increased, so that she who was going to have only a little pain, would have it increased because of the sin in having children: for they are born with groaning and sorrow, and those born are not regarded without grief. Now for the third time such a sentence is pronounced upon the man: “Because you have listened,” he says, “to the voice of your wife, and have eaten of the tree of which I commanded you not to eat, cursed is the earth in your works, and in sorrows you shall eat of it all the days of your life: thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you” (Gen. 3:17–18). And here too Adam is called back to that for which he had been made, but with a loss. For previously he had been placed to till the earth simply, so that the result of his labor might follow him; but when he despised God’s command, believing that by the serpent’s counsel things would be better provided for him than God had made them, he is recalled to his former appointment with the disadvantage of toil; so that the earth would by no means respond to him according to his labor, being cursed not for itself, but for his works, so that it might be shown that God’s purpose cannot be overthrown, nor can anyone provide better than God. For no one can love another’s work more than he who made it himself, as the Apostle says, because, he says, no one ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, as Christ also does the Church (Eph. 5:29). Let us now see whether the following things in the Law agree with its beginnings. When Abraham had pleased God, among the other things that pertain to the reward of his faith, although he was old, he was judged worthy to beget one son (Gen. 18:10). How then can it be blamed as though it were a reward granted, that God should fulfill the will of one who had done God’s own will? That will would not have been fulfilled unless it were harmless; nor would God fulfill what He saw was asked badly or ignorantly, especially by one who was pleasing to Him; for even a man should not do that. And Anna, though she was barren and loved God, asked to have a son and received one (1 Sam. 1); and if this had been something contrary, she could have been warned by Him whom she loved not to ask for a harmful thing. And Samuel, most holy, who was born from her, begot sons, yet did not lessen the merits of his righteousness. From his earliest years he was always advancing, so that in old age he might be praised by a fuller testimony of God. And Zacharias the priest, a just man, in his old age begot a son by God’s command; and before that son was born, he merited to prophesy (Luke 1:5). On what grounds, then, is that accused which is clearly shown not to be harmful? And who will deny that what harms no one ought to be called good? And to say something here about the Apostles, which pertains to strengthening the case: certainly Saint John was the guardian of chastity; but his fellow disciple, that is, Saint Peter, is known to have had a wife; and to receive the primacy among the Apostles, the begetting of children was no obstacle to him. How then can that be thought worthy of condemnation which does not hinder merit? Therefore the Apostle shows that one who has a wife, if he keeps the commandments in other respects, can and ought to be made a priest. For if it were unlawful, he certainly could not say that a sinner ought to be made a priest. And what is clearer? It is the voice of the same Apostle who says: “Concerning virgins I have no commandment of the Lord” (1 Cor. 7:25). For when the Corinthians were harassed by heretics who, in hypocrisy, taught that marriages must be condemned, they consulted the Apostle by letter whether it was permitted to marry or to dismiss a wife. Then the Apostle commanded that a wife ought not to depart from her husband; and when he had the occasion to say, if he had known that it should be taught so, that it is not permitted to marry, he showed that he could not teach what had not been handed down to him. But which of the disciples would teach what was not handed down by the Master? Or who would not listen to him preaching: “I want younger women to marry, to bear children” (1 Tim. 5:14)? But perhaps it may be said: If it is permitted and good to marry, why is it not permitted for priests to have wives? that is, that once ordained, they may no longer have marital relations? Who does not know that each state has its own law? For there are things which absolutely and generally are not permitted to all; there are also things which are permitted to some and not permitted to others; and there are things which are sometimes permitted and sometimes not permitted. Fornication is never permitted to anyone; trade, however, is sometimes permitted and sometimes not permitted. For before a man enters church office, he is permitted to trade; once he has become a cleric, it is no longer permitted. And for a Christian to have relations with his wife is sometimes permitted and sometimes not permitted. Because on days of solemn procession it is sometimes not permitted to have relations; since even lawful things must be abstained from, that what is asked may be more easily obtained. Therefore the Apostle says it is necessary to abstain for a time by mutual consent, that one may devote oneself to prayer (1 Cor. 7:5). For according to the Law, on a fast day it is not permitted to strike or to quarrel, afterwards it is permitted; because greater reverence is owed to the things of God. Is everything that is permitted before others permitted also before the emperor? How much more in the things of God? And therefore His bishop must be purer than others: for he seems to bear His person, being His vicar; so that what is permitted to others is not permitted to him, because he must of necessity daily act in the place of Christ, either to pray for the people, or to offer, or to baptize. And not only is intercourse forbidden to this man, but also to his minister: because he ought to be cleaner, since the things he ministers are holy. For just as, in comparison with a lamp, darkness is not only dim but also filthy, whereas in comparison with the stars a lamp is gloom, and in comparison with the sun the stars are murky, and in comparison with the brightness of God the sun is night; so also the things that are lawful and pure for us, in comparison with God’s dignity are as though unlawful and impure; for though they are good, they do not befit the person of God. Is not the tunic of a man of moderate station, though clean, yet filthy and unsuitable for an emperor? Likewise a Saxon cloak for a senator? And therefore the bishops of God must be purer than others, because they bear the person of Christ, and the ministers of God must be cleaner. For no one serves the emperor without carefulness; therefore they serve clothed in bright and clean garments. But because God by nature is most radiant, it is necessary that His ministers be clean by nature rather than by garments; to whom be praise and glory for ever and ever. Amen.

(Genesis 3:1) 

1ST CATEGORY OT

QUESTION 31. WHETHER, WITH THE WOMAN, A SERPENT SPOKE ACCORDING TO ITS NATURE, OR WHETHER THE SERPENT, ACTUALLY MEANING THE DEVIL, DECEIVED HER? — As far as the historical account is concerned, the serpent is called such by nature, being said to be wiser than all the other beasts that the Lord God had made upon the earth. Indeed, God even pronounced a sentence upon the serpent. For what wonder is it if the Devil was wiser than the beasts, of whom the Apostle says among other things, “Do you not know the depths of Satan?” (2 Cor. 2:11). Moreover, it was so truly a serpent by nature that it was told, “Upon your breast and belly you shall crawl, and dust you shall eat all the days of your life” (Gen. 3:14). These things are far removed from the condition of Satan, because he is neither bodily nor mortal. And if the sentence is considered in itself, it will be seen that the sentence given has not harmed the serpent: rather, it was commanded to remain in that state in which it was made. For since it was made a servant of Satan for the overthrow of man, to whom God had subjected all things, God, in that very subjection in which He had subjected all things to man, repressed the pride of the serpent, by which it had begun to be the agent of arrogance. For man seemed to have been placed beneath the serpent, through whom, after receiving counsel, he despised the law given to him. And since serpents are wise, the Lord confirms this in the Gospel, saying, “Be wise as serpents” (Matt. 10:16). Therefore, since it is clear that a true serpent spoke with Eve, what remains is to discern whether it could have been so wise and cunning as to deceive her by trickery. For if it was more wise than the other beasts, it was not, however, more wise than human beings, since no animal is rational except man. Therefore it is impossible that the serpent itself devised such subtlety: although it is called wise, it is not so beyond its nature. For it does not deliberate or devise or take counsel. Therefore, that it was the Devil who through the serpent bypassed the woman is beyond doubt. By associating himself with the serpent, he acted through it as through an instrument, so that the woman would not recognize the hidden deceit of the Devil, knowing that the serpent was wise. And therefore, though the sentence was given in a bodily form, it fell spiritually upon Satan, because a sentence holds the guilty party. For the sentence was not given by man, who might perhaps destroy an innocent person through error or ill will, but by God, who certainly cannot be deceived, so that His sentence binds only him who is guilty. Since Satan is invisible, yet worked his deceit bodily, the sentence appears to have been given bodily, so that it might spiritually bind him whose deed brought about the pronouncement of the sentence. For Satan, having been cast out from the most sacred dwellings of heaven, thrashes upon the earth, always groaning in utmost shamelessness. But it may perhaps be asked, In what language do you think the serpent spoke to the woman? Surely with the serpent’s own mouth. For even today there are people who understand the barking of dogs, the howling of wolves, the trumpeting of elephants, and the crowing of roosters; why then could not the still unrefined woman know and understand the hissing of serpents, since we know many people who can distinguish the voices of birds? And it is also certain that the Devil uses the tongue of that body into which he has entered; otherwise he could not have deceived the woman. And therefore, he spoke through the serpent with the serpent’s mouth.

(Genesis 3:7-9)

1ST CATEGORY OT

QUESTION 19. WAS ADAM'S BODY, WHEN IT WAS CREATED, IMMORTAL OR SUBJECT TO DEATH? — God made man in such a way that, as long as he did not sin, he would flourish in immortality: so that he himself would be the author for himself either of life or of death; that by guarding himself from sin, he would, by his own effort, rejoice that he was immortal; but by becoming careless, he would blame himself, because he had begun to be mortal. For as long as he continued in the law of his Creator, he was worthy to eat from the tree of life, so that he could not die. For his body was not of such a kind that it would seem impossible for it to be dissolved; rather, the taste of the tree of life restrained the body’s corruption. Indeed, even after the sin, it could have remained everlasting, if only it had been permitted him to eat from the tree of life. For how could he have had an immortal body if it was sustained by food? For the immortal does not need food or drink. Food supplied strength, while the tree of life, in the manner of a medicine, prevented all corruption. Therefore it was for man as though it were an secure wall.

(Genesis 4:1-18)

1ST CATEGORY OT

QUESTION 5. WHY WAS ABEL’S SACRIFICE ACCEPTED, AND CAIN’S REJECTED? — This can be gathered from the words of the very passage itself, since the story is not wrapped in literary pretense. For Scripture’s own language shows Abel to be wise and devout in what he did, but Cain careless and thoughtless, and therefore less devout. Abel, then, chose the better parts from the peaceful flock to offer to the Lord his creator, so that from the things God had created he might offer Him the worthiest, thereby proving both his own submission and God’s merit, and showing his personal reverence and God as author of all. Cain, crudely, was unable to present this. Fixing his whole mind in the soil, he could not lift the eyes of his heart to heaven to see what would be worthy of the Creator; he offered whatever gifts to God, of whatever sort they were. The same cause is found in the Jews with their crooked minds. They were often criticized when they carelessly offered their own gifts to God’s altar, gifts that did not even seem worthy of men, while the Lord said, “You offer to me the blind and the lame; I will not receive these from your hands. Offer them to your governor or your leader, if he will accept them” (Mal. 1:8). It is agreed among all that the greatest gifts ought to be offered to a person of high rank. Therefore Cain’s gifts were rejected, as the Lord said to him, “Why are you downcast, and why has your face fallen? If you offer rightly, but do not divide rightly, have you not sinned? Be calm. Its turning is toward you, and you shall rule over it” (Gen. 4:6–7). You see, then, that division suffers sin, since, without considering what was worthy of God, he kept the better part for his own use. Therefore he is not criticized because he offered, but because he offered unworthy things. Nor is he condemned on that account, but because, when warned, he refused to correct what he had done. For, “Its turning,” He says, “is toward you, and you shall rule over it”: that is, since I do not accept it, the gift you have offered is turned back to your own control, so that from then on you might know what you should do. From this envy flared up so that he killed his brother, so that the unrighteous man killed the one who had first shown righteousness, and a bad example might be given to mankind. Therefore, blinded by the rivalry of jealousy, he not only failed to give thanks that he had not been made guilty, and had learned how to correct this, but even added something worse by which he would deserve condemnation. Such is the case of careless and murderous Cain, like that of the wicked servant who, though his master had forgiven him, went out ungrateful and throttled his fellow servant, so that he might be condemned without excuse both for the past crime forgiven him and for his cruelty against his fellow servant (Matt. 18:27). And yet Cain was not at that moment condemned, but, shamed and guilty, was sent forth under terror upon the earth, so that, if he repented, he might be forgiven. Fearing that someone might kill him for this deed, he said to the Lord, “My case is too great for me to be left; if you cast me out today from your face, I shall hide myself from the face of the earth, and I shall be groaning and trembling upon the earth. And whoever finds me will kill me.” (Gen. 4:14) Terrified, then, by the words of the just Judge, Cain fears being despised by the Lord, so much so that he thinks he must flee even from the sight of men; knowing that whoever lives under God’s wrath may also be killed by man. But what does the Lord answer him? “Not so,” He says—that is, I did not spare you, though you do not deserve to live, so that you might be killed by someone; but so that you might groan and tremble, as one who first gave an evil example upon the earth, when the fruit from the ground does not answer to your labors. Therefore He says, “Whoever kills Cain will pay sevenfold vengeance.” (Gen. 4:15) This sentence shows that Cain is rightly to be condemned. For when he saw that a law was given with such a threat, so that no one should imitate his deed, he began to fear more, knowing what evil he had committed. So God promises sevenfold vengeance if anyone should aspire to this crime, so that, seeing that Cain had been made guilty by this act, and while the revelation of the law was not yet clear, he might know that he would be punished sevenfold if he did not avoid it; so that the knowledge of the law would add six plagues beyond what Cain had deserved, and with Cain’s plague the vengeance would be counted as seven. By this same number those are to be rewarded who leave all things and follow the Lord, and in the future will have eternal life. This is the sign the Lord set upon Cain, lest anyone who found him should kill him (Gen. 4:13–15). In the case of a murder, a law has been set that if anyone commits homicide, since every murder is homicide, he shall be seven times more guilty than Cain was, so that, terrified by such severity, others may restrain themselves from this crime.

(Genesis 4:23)

1ST CATEGORY OT

QUESTION 6. DID LAMECH KILL CAIN, AS SOME THINK? — Those who think this are mistaken, believing that when Lamech spoke of Cain he meant, “I killed a man who hurt me, a young man who covered me with wounds.” (Gen. 4:24) By then Lamech had already been born in the fifth generation from Cain, that is, from Methuselah, Cain’s great‑grandson. Lamech mentions this to show that anyone who sins under a revealed law must be bound more strictly. And therefore, if after Cain his imitator was avenged seven times, how much more must vengeance be taken on the one whom neither Cain’s deed and correction, nor the sentence afterward passed on him, was able to terrify, so as to turn his will away from so wicked and cruel a crime? Therefore, after Cain, Lamech committed this murder, and undoubtedly, in line with what was said above, he paid sevenfold vengeance. And he shows what would happen after Lamech to whoever followed his example, when he says, “But on Lamech seventy‑seven times” (Gen. 4:23–24). Since a wicked deed not followed by repentance is struck with seventy‑seven blows of punishment, therefore also the Savior commanded that one who sins seventy‑seven times, if he turns back, is yet to be forgiven (Matt. 18:22). But so that no one may think another committed murder after Cain and before Lamech, because Lamech said, “Cain is avenged” (Gen. 4:24, according to the LXX), as though it had already happened: how could Lamech say of himself that vengeance had already been taken on him, when the murder he confessed to committing was still recent? For it is certain that every act carries its sentence with it. When there is no other expectation than that, once the deed is complete, its due recompense is known, the future is considered as already done. Indeed it was said to Adam and Eve, “On the day you eat of it, you shall die by death” (Gen. 2:17); and certainly they did not die immediately, but after a long interval of time. Yet because they had already lost the hope of immortality, their future death was called present, since it began to be held in view as certain. Therefore, since Lamech admits that he killed a young man, and since it is clear that Cain could not have lived until that time, or if he did, which seems impossible, he would have been older, Lamech did not kill him.

(Genesis 6:3)

2ND CATEGORY OT

QUESTION 5. WHY DOES GOD SAY, “MY SPIRIT SHALL NOT REMAIN IN THESE MEN, BECAUSE THEY ARE FLESH; THEIR YEARS SHALL BE ONE HUNDRED AND TWENTY,” ETC. (Gen. 6:3)? —  Since in those days there were giants upon the earth, lethal and proud, arrogant by the greatness of their stature, following the desires of the flesh, born apostates; then, when this displeased God, He promised that He would destroy the human race by a flood and set a time, so that if anyone, upon hearing of God’s wrath and anger in this matter, should wish to correct himself, he would have a span of time to reform. In fact, the ark seems for this reason to have been built over a hundred years. But it is said that twenty years elapsed before the beginning of the ark. Yet the narrative, by what it adds after mentioning the number of Noah’s years, seems to obscure this. For this decree is understood to have been issued before Noah was five hundred years old. For what does it say? “My Spirit shall not remain in these men”; and therefore it adds, “Because wickedness has increased upon the earth, I will blot out man from the face of the earth, down to cattle”; which certainly was fulfilled when the flood took place. For even after the flood we remember that men lived many years: and it is recorded that Aaron, the brother of Moses, lived one hundred and twenty-three years (Num. 33:38–39). But Moses himself, so that he could not pass beyond one hundred and twenty years, brought it about that he did not glorify God at the waters of contradiction. For he was to enter into the land of promise, had not sin stood in the way (Deut. 34:7 and 32:48–52). For it seems to some that this statement was made with reference to the time of Moses, since we find that Jehoiada the priest lived one hundred and thirty years (2 Chron. 24:15).

(Genesis 11:14-21). 

1ST CATEGORY NT

QUESTION 108. ON THE HEBREW LANGUAGE, WHERE IT TOOK ITS NAME. — Everything that is from God is rational, and for each thing its origin gives the reason why it exists, so that it may not seem to be named or to subsist without sense, but may show a designation which is understood to be the head, as it were, of its own name. Therefore the reason of a man is the cause by which he stands. Now he stands from four elements, namely earth, air, water, and fire, with God alone as author; the fifth is the soul, as it were a charioteer, to drive the material and shaped body, and as its commander. And from the ground [humus] we have taken our beginning, and from its name we are called. For we are called “men” [homines] because of the ground [humus], from which our father has his external origin. Therefore cause and reason bring it about that from the name of one person the others subsisting under the same name are called by it, signifying him in themselves. Accordingly, let us see whether it fits, as some think, that the Hebrews are so called from Heber. For as far as the name is concerned, the origin of this name seems to descend from him; for Heber is earlier than Abraham. But if this were true, those who are of the tribe of Heber ought, after him, to be called by the same name; for from Heber Abraham was born in the seventh generation (Gen. 11:16, 26). If therefore, after Abraham, or Abraham himself, was called a Hebrew, then without doubt the Hebrews are named from Heber; but if it is not read that they were called Hebrews in the time of Abraham, but after Abraham, then clearly they are not said to be from Heber, but from Abraham: since the sons of Abraham are known to have been first called by this name. For in Genesis Joseph and his brothers are called Hebrews (Gen. 43:32). For knowing that Abraham was he who had come down from Syria into Canaan (Gen. 12:4), and had been multiplied, being filled with all resources for the sake of faith, called king and prophet and father of many nations (Gen. 17:4), who with his three hundred and eighteen home-born servants struck down five kings (Gen. 14:14–15); since these things were not done and spoken in a corner, so as to be hidden, they called those who were of his seed Hebrews. It belonged therefore to the rank and merit of Abraham that he should become the head of those who draw their lineage from him. For by God’s judgment he was placed as prince and origin in the land of Canaan, so that those born from him should have another profession and way of life than he had before he went down into the land of Canaan; for he, being renewed, should establish a new people in devotion to God. Therefore it is that the apostle Paul confesses himself to be “a Hebrew of Hebrews” (Phil. 3:5); for this seemed to be a title of dignity. It was a testimony and nobility of lineage that they should be surnamed from his name, who had pleased God in many ways and who was their source. Let this be rejected if it does not agree with reason; let it be despised if it is unlike; let it be torn up if it is foreign to the merits of Abraham; and let us be refuted as his flatterers. What hostility is this against Abraham, what rivalry, by which his enemies belittle him? And who are these, if not those who are called his sons? In what respect does Abraham displease them, that this glory should be thought unfamiliar to him? And what is there in Heber to please them, that he should be said to have this primacy? If his way of life could be investigated, it would perhaps be found that he worshipped idols, like Thare and Nachor and the father of Nachor, who clearly were not far from him, as Joshua testifies, who says they worshipped idols (Josh. 24:2). Or at least let those who are on the other side show by what reasoning this must be claimed for Heber, lest perhaps we suppress his merit; but there is none, because the Scriptures are common to us all, and it is in the open what is owed to each. For if they think this ought to be defended from the name alone, it is weak and unlikely. It would then rightly be vindicated for his name if there were some proofs of causes which confirmed this: for some people of the same name could claim as theirs what does not belong to them. And therefore this is true, because it is established not only by the name, but also by clear reasoning. For since by God’s gracious choice it was brought about that in Abraham the human race should be made alive, and that he should become a saving pattern for men, it is not doubtful to anyone that in him was restored that which had been lost through the fault of human frailty. For he was set as a certain image, that after his likeness the human race might return to God, so that both the worship of God and the word which had previously been given for the use of men might be restored to humankind: because as in the beginning in Adam there was the image of God, so that God might be known on earth, so after the ruins of the human race and the forgetfulness of the true God, in Abraham it was refashioned, so that from him faith in God might begin, and again sprout forth into fruit. Where it is not unreasonable that from his name the people that began from him should obtain their designation. But lest perhaps they suffer doubt because of the name Heber, since the name Heber sounds closer to “Hebrews,” because they are called Hebrews, not Abraheans, let them notice again that they are called Hebrews, not Heberaeans: for he was called Heber, not Hebre. If therefore they think this point must be attacked from here, they suffer what they do, and neither of us will have the victory on this side, except the one who, by giving a reason in order, shows that what he asserts is true. For he who is equal in one matter must be said to have lost if he is found unequal in another. For the letter was changed because of the sound, so that they should say “Hebraei” instead of “Hebrei,” because it sounds better. For also from Juda they are not called “Judai” but “Judaei.” For wherever it seemed awkward, the letter was changed, so that the word might have a harmonious sound. For instead of medio die, we say meridie, and there are many such cases. Therefore it is fitting, as has been shown, that from the name of Abraham both the language and the people should be named. This, then, is the language which we say was first given to Adam and the others, which, because of the presumption shown in building the tower, we believe was scattered into many and confused, so that no longer this one language, but many derived from it, came to exist through the alteration of certain expressions: so that they would have one appearance, and yet it would not be lost, but would be completely mixed in with the other languages. For this was done then, so that people would not understand one another and dare greater things (Gen. 11:8). Therefore, it is understood that as many languages then existed as there were people who, being scattered, each in the places where they lived, established a language of their own. But if this is not thought to be the very language which is written to have been then the one language, it will remain to be said that it was gathered bit by bit from the other languages and fitted together into the form of a single language which Abraham used; so that, because he was the father of many nations, he would have a speech composed from many languages, and would be wholly renewed in every respect. But since those whom the Book of Genesis mentions as of one voice and speech (Gen. 11:31), are read to have migrated from the East, and then again to have been scattered by God over the face of the whole earth, that language certainly did not remain there, so that the language first given should remain. Indeed, it does not have any land among humankind, as the other languages do, nor any nation, except the Jews; because it was given to the first man in Paradise. And after the languages were confused, this language, which is now called Hebrew, was nowhere to be found. If, then, it has nowhere a place or a nation; and Abraham was by race a Syrian; where came this language to Abraham or to the rest of his offspring, unless because it is either that first language, or at least put together from many? For we see that some languages have certain words similar to it. But this does not so well accord with reason as the other view, if it is said to be itself the first: reason shows that this was not done without purpose. Abraham ought to have had the very language which the first man had, so that Moses, when he came to describe the creation and man made by God, would use that speech with which God spoke and named the man Adam, and Adam’s wife was called Eve: so that this speech would be in the book of Moses, which had also been in those whom he describes, so that he might truly show in all things the re-establishment of the first cause and the divine favor in Abraham.

(Genesis 11)

1ST CATEGORY NT

QUESTION 117. ON ABRAHAM. — The faith of this patriarch was so exceptional and wondrous that all other righteous people confess him, by God’s judgment, as the father of belief; nor is anyone worthy of and dear to God unless he is called his son. The right of his honor and value is faith, which he does not hesitate to give even to incredible things, and among other privileges he was also found worthy to see the Savior in hope of the future Incarnation, as the Lord said and proved to the Jews: Your father Abraham rejoiced that he might see my day; and he saw it and was glad (Jn. 8:56). For since he became father by the value of faith, it was fitting that he should foresee the hope of his future children, which, through the gracious and provident God, would overflow from a human and devout father upon his obedient sons as an inheritance. Let us now see what this faith believed, so that it reached such honor and glory by divine judgment. We have praised the faith, but we have not yet said what it believed. For the Lord, leading him out, showed him the stars of heaven and said: If you can, number them. So shall your seed be. And Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness (Gen. 15:5–6). It would not be a great thing to have believed God, except that what he believed the world judges not to be believed and as foolish, because this is not within the hope of things according to nature. Therefore Abraham, being one out of the world because he believed this, was separated from worldly people and justified. Therefore, believing this is made great by the unbelieving wisdom of the world, and to have believed against its hope is of the highest value. For the despair of worldly men is the value and hope of Christians. For the cause of evil becomes the reward of good: faith is stronger and fuller when it commits itself more to things that are incredible. A man already dried up and from an aged wife believed he would have seed so abundant that it could not be numbered; looking not so much at what was shown, but at him who showed it, not thinking that he could lie. And therefore it was counted to him for righteousness. For it is dull to believe a thing absurd and known to be impossible, unless there is a person who persuades us to believe it. Therefore Abraham is admirable for his faith and for the discernment of his heart, since he both believes that which is incredible and commits himself to him to whom not to believe is both foolish and dangerous. This shows our faith to be reasonable, that it believes this not of any other than of God, that he is able to do what he promises. This, then, is the bulwark of faith, this its triumph. Seeing this, some wise men of the world, because the nature of things cannot do this, say it is foolish to believe. Ignorant that, according to the Apostle, what is foolish of God is wiser than men (1 Cor. 1:25). For they would rightly judge us foolish if we believed of the nature of things what is proved not to be possible. But we, on the contrary, believe that God will be able to do what nature cannot, if he has promised it. What folly can be found in this matter? If, however, the work which is believed possible is unworthy of God, then faith is rightly compared to dullness; but if it is worthy, precisely because it is impossible to the creature, why is the faith not to be praised which attributes so much to the Creator as the creature is denied power to do? Great and admirable, then, is Abraham, who did not doubt to believe God against the world’s judgment, because he can do what he promises. A Chaldean by birth, he appears as a master of belief: though skilled in astrology, he still placed God above human counsel, judging it fitting that such things be believed of God as cannot be investigated in respect to how they may come to pass. For he strengthened his own weakness by the power of God, since God determined, to proclaim the unique greatness of his majesty, to perform things that are impossible and unheard of to the world; and by doing this he would show himself Lord of the creature, and the creature would subject itself to him whose work would seem impossible to all others; by whose unbelief the most faithful Abraham is raised higher. For his faith is the punishment of unbelievers; the deceit of unbelievers is his glory. For he is the father of the faithful and the judge of the unfaithful. By his example, the good are granted eternal life, and the wicked will receive eternal punishments. In that time, when the world was still small in knowledge and not yet enlightened by signs and wonders that might draw it to faith, he did not deny faith to God against his own understanding. Therefore holy Abraham was given as a most faithful example to the human race. In him all nations were prefigured as coming to salvation through faith; and that the overflowing increase of his faith might be known, he is tested and ordered to sacrifice his son to God, a thing that had never before been done, and he is neither disturbed by the novelty of the deed nor does he dispute whether a murder ought to be committed at God’s command, he who had threatened that murder must not be committed. Therefore, fearless and secure about the will of God, he does not hesitate to think that what God commands is provident: and this son, whom two old people received through a promise, the reward of faith, the witness of virtues, and in whom all hope of the promised future seed was held. That he might fulfill this with complete devotion, he did not tell his mother, lest she bring some obstacle to his obedience, knowing that mothers are the more inclined in love toward the affection they bear for their children; therefore he concealed it from her, not doubting that what God commands must be fulfilled, so that by this example we might be taught to carry out God’s commands with all carefulness. For if the most faithful Abraham is found obedient in a matter so grave and harsh, how much more should we, to whom things are commanded that can be accepted? O faith dedicated to God, and hope firm in the Lord, which is so dear and sweet that it is preferred to the affections of parents and children, as Scripture says: Taste and see, that the Lord is sweet (Ps. 33:9)! But our patriarch, most faithful Abraham, because he was a prophet, knew what was to follow. Therefore, in accordance with what the Lord had just said, he then acted, so that he preferred God in love over his son, dear as he was, with the Lord saying, “If anyone loves father or mother, or children more than me, he is not worthy of me” (Matt. 10:37). Therefore the Patriarch, in order to be found worthy of the Lord above all others, did not refuse even to kill his son.

(Genesis 13:5-18) 

1ST CATEGORY OT

QUESTION 44. HOW COULD IT BE SHOWN FROM THE TESTIMONY OF THE PROPHETS, ALREADY RECEIVED AMONG THE GENTILES IN THE NEW TESTAMENT, THAT THE PROMISE WHICH GOD MADE TO ABRAHAM HAS BEEN FULFILLED THROUGH THE COMING OF CHRIST? — It is written in the prophet Isaiah: “My house shall be called a house of prayer for all nations” (Isa. 56:7). But perhaps the Jews will say: The house of God, that is, the synagogue, is open to all. Nor do we object; yet in such a way that, as always, the circumcised join themselves to the Law. For their Law is that by which they were commanded, after the manner of Abraham, to be circumcised. Therefore, nothing new can seem to be signified by this example of the prophet; since anyone coming from any nation has never been forbidden from the beginning of Judaism to join himself to the Law. Nothing new spoken by the prophet can be thought, indeed it would be unessential, if the Gentiles have always been admitted to serve the God of Abraham and are never found to have been forbidden. And this is true, because those who submit themselves to the Law are never found not to have been received. If, therefore, these things are so, it seems needless that the prophet admonished about what, once handed down, has always been observed. And could anyone so dull be found as to say that the prophet spoke something unnecessary and empty? I do not know for whom it would be safe even to hear this and not oppose it. For since the Jewish people, on account of the sins which they committed against God, seeking help from idols, were often rebuked by the prophets but refused to enter upon the path of repentance so as to return to God, God, in reproach of them, indicated that He would open His house to all nations to pray, so that, the Jews being cast off, He would show that He would place others in their place. For if the nations have always been admitted to the Law, as was said above, how could the prophet say that this would happen in the future, unless he meant something different from what had been previously commanded? He could not speak of a thing which was done daily as though it were going to come. Therefore it is clear that this tends to the ruin of the Jews, to whom the prophet shows that, with them removed, others were to be called and were to receive the house of God’s grace, which had been promised to the Jews. What that promise is, the prophet Isaiah teaches, saying: “There shall come out of Zion one who shall deliver and shall turn away ungodliness from Jacob; and this shall be my covenant with them” (Isa. 59:20–21). Therefore this covenant is the removal of sins. This is the New Covenant, which was promised through Jeremiah, who says: “Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will accomplish for the house of Israel and the house of Judah a new covenant, not according to the covenant which I arranged for their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt; for they did not continue in my covenant, and I neglected them, says the Lord” (Jer. 31:31–32). This is their transgression, when they made the image of a calf; then they corrupted His covenant. Therefore also the tablets on which the Law had been given were shattered under the mountain (Exod. 32:4, 19), because they deserved to receive more severe precepts. But because God is mild and merciful, He promised through the prophets that He would change the Law, so as to give another Covenant, which would differ from that which He had given before: that not only what was burdensome might be changed, but also those things which were given in figure, that is, the sabbath and circumcision; so that, since they had long been oppressed, being relieved in all things, they might give grateful thanks to God as petitioners. And because, persisting in their fathers’ transgression, they refused to turn their minds away from idols, He testifies that the nations, together with the remnant who kept the faith, will enjoy the Covenant which He had said would come: so that the faithless Jews might be tortured in a twofold way. For they were burdened for a time by the precepts, and in the future they will pay fitting penalties, because they were found faithful neither in the Old nor in the New Covenant. So He said that He would give a New Covenant, so that the Old, which had been given to the Fathers, would cease. And therefore, whoever serves God in this Covenant does not observe the sabbath, nor new moons, nor circumcision, nor distinctions of foods; but has only the fear of God in faith: because he will not be justified by the Law, but by faith, as the prophet Habakkuk says: “For the righteous shall live by faith” (Hab. 2:4); so that he no longer uses many precepts to gain favor with God, but few. Isaiah again, speaking with the same meaning, says: “Though the number of the sons of Israel be as the sand of the sea, a remnant of them shall be saved. For the Lord shall accomplish and cut short His word in righteousness, because the Lord will make a short word upon the whole earth” (Isa. 10:22–23). For the remnant who will persevere in the faith of the promise, while the others do not believe, He shows the shortened word of the Law: this is the New Covenant which He promised. It would not otherwise be called a Covenant, unless in a similar way this too were confirmed by the witness of blood, just as the Old Covenant, so that both might have one and the same name: but in the Old, many precepts, in the New, however, few, as He promised. So that, since He had said that Abraham would be the father of many nations (Gen. 17:4–5), in the same way the sons might be justified as the father had been justified: so that, once those things ceased which began after the faith of Abraham, those who receive the faith by which that same Abraham was justified might be sons of Abraham, as was said by the Lord. And this is neither strange nor unheard of, that men should be justified without care for the sabbath and circumcision and the rest of the commandments of this sort. For Enoch did not please God by this, that he might be translated; nor was Noah found righteous in the flood by observing this alone; nor was Abraham himself justified after he was circumcised: “Abraham,” it says, “believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Heb. 11:5, 7, 8; Rom. 4:3). Then he was circumcised, so that there might be in him a sign that, though he was old, he believed that he would have a son. Therefore it is not circumcision that commends Abraham, but faith. And so, for those who believe, faith is sufficient for justification, that they may be sons of Abraham in faith, not in circumcision, because they have no need of circumcision. For what Abraham believed is not what is believed in their case. But the Jews were therefore ordered to be circumcised, so that they might have the sign of Abraham’s faith, not of their own faith, but so that they might be known as his sons according to the flesh. Yet if they believe, they will be his sons also in justification. For what advantage is it to be called the son of a powerful man if one is powerless, except that it is even more harmful? For it is a disgrace to be the son of a noble and glorious man without honor. Indeed, bodily circumcision is so far from being a merit that God says through the prophet Jeremiah that He will take vengeance on all the circumcised in foreskin, if they are not circumcised in heart (Jer. 4:4). Yet He is not angry with those who are circumcised in heart but uncircumcised in flesh, because no one has ever pleased God without the circumcision of the heart. Whoever, therefore, are circumcised in the flesh signify the lineage of Abraham according to the flesh; but those who are circumcised in heart signify the lineage of God according to faith, because, being circumcised from all worldly error, they confess God as their Father. What then does the circumcision of the flesh profit, if, when faith is lacking in the Jew, he cannot attain to the merit of Abraham? Or what harm is there in foreskin, when no one attains to his righteousness except the one who has followed the faith of Abraham? They therefore glory in the circumcision of the flesh in vain, since they see that it has no merit before God. And since, as has been shown, it is better to have faith than circumcision, the Gentiles are better than the Jews; for the Gentiles have faith, the Jews have circumcision. And whom do you think He recognizes more as sons of Abraham: those who are like him according to the flesh, or those who are like him in faith? But the faith of Abraham bears witness. And therefore he glories not in the flesh but in faith. For this reason he has received as sons those whom he sees to be imitators of his glory. For how can he call those sons from whom he sees a shrinking back from that by which he pleased God and was justified? He will therefore be able to judge them not as his sons, but as his enemies. For they appear to be envious of him, despising the faith through which he was glorified. Nor is it surprising if the Jews are found untrusting, not at all accepting the New Testament, when we know that they were not faithful even in the Old.
