Or shall Samson be called worthy because the Spirit of the Lord came upon him while he was consorting with prostitutes (Judg. 14:6, 19; 15:14), when this is to be understood as done for the destruction of the Philistines?

1 SAMUEL

(1 Samuel 7:9) 

1ST CATEGORY OT

QUESTION 46. WHETHER SAMUEL WAS ONE OF THE SONS OF AARON, AND WHETHER HE IS TO BE CONSIDERED A PRIEST? — There are some among us who, partly occupied with secular affairs and partly less studious concerning the Holy Scriptures, fall into error, thinking that Samuel was a priest, that is, that he traced his origin from Aaron, whose offspring the Lord God ordained should be born priests, not made priests. Nor was it granted to anyone except his sons to place incense on the altar. Some, going even further astray, indeed deny that Samuel was of the line of Aaron; that is, they say he was not born a priest, and nevertheless assert that he exercised the priesthood. These must first be answered. For it is worse to deny that Samuel was born a priest and yet claim that he exercised the priesthood, than to say he was a priest from among the sons of Aaron. In the latter case it is ignorance; in the former, foolishness. For when those who think he was born a priest learn that he was not of the sons of Aaron, they will clearly see that he was not a priest, being unaware that no one was permitted to perform any priestly act unless he was of the seed of Aaron. For they know the established fact, indeed it is evident, that Korah, since he was not of the sons of Aaron and wanted to place incense upon the altar, was swallowed up with his associates by the opening of the earth (Num. 16:1–34). And Uzziah the king, since he was certainly not of the seed of Aaron but of the tribe of Judah, and boldly undertook to perform priestly functions while standing before the altar, was struck with leprosy on his forehead and therefore died (2 Chron. 26:16–21). But those who say that Samuel was not born a priest and nonetheless assert that he exercised the priesthood speak quite foolishly; and to persuade a fool of what is good is the greatest labor. For with what dullness are they led, that, while the sun is shining upon the earth, they say that it is night? For when they read, and they read this not in one place only, that it is decreed by God that no one should dare to exercise the priesthood except Aaron and his sons, they stubbornly contend that Samuel was a priest. They do not understand that if Samuel was not born a priest and yet exercised the priesthood, he must be called a shameless pretender; for God established that priests should be born, not made. And I think it is not safe to hold this opinion about Samuel. For how could it be that a praiseworthy man, praised by God’s own testimony, did what he knew was forbidden? He was certainly aware of the punishment for such belief, having seen it carried out once and again. Nor could he have sought to this by God’s judgment, whom he knew to be binding; if he had perhaps heard such a thing from God, he would rather have believed himself to be tested, knowing that God’s decree in no way can be revoked. He could more likely have believed that, under the appearance and name of God, this was being done with him in order that he be deceived by the adversary, than that God could change His judgment. Indeed, when Balaam had been forbidden by God to go to Balak, and later asked again whether he should go, God, angered with him, rebuked him through the mouth of a donkey, because the donkey, seeing the angel who was forbidding the way, refused to continue the journey begun (Num. 22:28). But Balaam, though forbidden by God to go, asked again whether He wished him to go, and therefore judged of God as of a man, who through his ignorance is changeable and alterable. Yet Balaam is nowhere praised by any divine testimony; for he was a soothsayer. But Samuel, a man dear to God and knowing that God’s judgments are fixed, how could he believe that anything should be done other than what he knew was established by God? “But,” they say, “when Eli died, and his sons who were priests, Samuel began to exercise the priesthood.” This neither the text teaches nor reason admits. In saying this, they suppose that at that time there was no one left to perform the priesthood, so that when those three were dead, unless Samuel offered the people’s gifts, the priesthood would have ceased to be exercised. This claim is hostile to God. By it God is judged negligent, as though ignorant, since He establishes something that cannot endure. For why did He decree that no one other than the sons of Aaron should exercise the priesthood until the end of the age, that is, until the times of the coming of Christ, if He knew this would fail? But if He did not know, which be far from us to say, then He was negligent; and therefore it could have happened that, when those failed, not even Samuel was a priest. But if God is provident and foreknowing, what He established remained in force; and if what He established remained in force, Samuel did not exercise the priesthood, since he was not God’s priest. For in the Old Law God decreed that priests should be born; in the New Law the Lord ordered that priests should be made. Let them now choose one of two: either prove Samuel to have been born a priest, or made a priest. Yet they agree that he was not born a priest, because they know he was not of the sons of Aaron. If therefore Samuel was not born a priest and is nowhere read or proved to have been made a priest, since God had not ordained that priests should be made, it is absolutely clear that Samuel was by no means a priest. But the objectors, with their eyes closed, say: “If he was not a priest, yet he acted in the stead of a priest, because it is written that he offered a sacrifice to God.” Who would dare deny what is proved by Scripture (1 Sam. 7:9)? Samuel indeed offered a sacrifice to God, but from this it is not shown that he acted in the position of a priest. For he is always said to offer whose offerings they are that the priest places upon the altar. And Saul offered in this very manner, that is, through a priest, just as sacrifices are now offered; and David offered, and Solomon offered, and the others likewise offered. Did they all act in the position of a priest? Although the priest performs his own proper office, yet he is said to offer in whose name the priest acts. The offering is accounted to the one whose gifts are presented. And if a man was not a priest, how could he act in the stead of a priest? Can a deacon act in the position of a priest? A captain may indeed act in the position of another captain, and a magistrate in the position of another magistrate; yet a private person cannot act in the position of any authority. How much less can one who is not a priest act in the position of a priest? With what reasoning would he dare desire to that which he knows is not permitted to him? For if a priest is lacking in some place, a priest from another place can be asked to come and take his place; yet a prophet, even if he lives a holy life, cannot perform what he knows has by no means been granted to him. For it is one thing to live well, and another to receive the authority of a certain office. Just as someone who is a priest ought not to think that his life is thereby automatically worthy, so also someone of holy conduct and life ought not on that basis claim the priesthood for himself. For although the priesthood is a good thing, it will nevertheless be evil for the one to whom it has not been granted and who ventures upon it. For if we look at what is written about the holy Samuel, we shall see what testimony Scripture gives him, saying: “And it became known,” it says, “to all the people that Samuel was faithful as a prophet to the Lord” (1 Sam. 3:20). And in the Psalm: “Moses and Aaron among his priests, and Samuel among those who call upon his name” (Ps. 98:6). Who does not notice from this distinction that the persons are separated on account of their dignities, so that Moses and Aaron are recognized as having obtained priestly dignity, whereas Samuel is regarded as having been worthy before God among the prophets, who by their prayers called upon God to protect his people, as we read? Moreover, priests are shown to have by no means been lacking, to such an extent that, when the Ark had been brought back from the Philistines by the Levite bearers, the men of Beth-shemesh offered sacrifices to God in Samuel’s absence. And when Saul had been made king, Ahimelech was the great-grandson of Eli the priest, who carried the vestment. “But here,” they say, “Samuel seems to have been a priest because he was clothed with a vestment.” As though deacons today are not vested with dalmatics, just as bishops are. And we read that David too was clothed with a vestment, and with a double vestment (2 Sam. 6:14). But Samuel, while still a little boy, was girded with a vestment (1 Sam. 2:18): could a little boy offer to God the people’s gifts? You see therefore that “vestment” is indeed one word, but it does not always signify one and the same thing. For priests carried the vestment; they were not clothed with it. Kings, however, and the Levite Samuel were clothed with the vestment. Therefore sometimes “vestment” signifies a garment, sometimes a sort of small chest which the priests carried for inquiring of the Lord.   So far as appears, it has been proven that Samuel was not a priest, but a prophet. Now we answer those who, not knowing that Samuel was not of the sons of Aaron the priest, suppose that he was a priest; for it would not have been lawful that someone descended from the line of Aaron should not be a priest. I want such people first to recognize that, if Samuel was a priest, then without doubt Elkanah his father was also a priest; it would likewise have been fitting that his sons be priests. But because they were not priests, he appointed them judges over the sons of Israel (1 Sam. 8:1), just as Samuel himself was. For we read that he judged the sons of Israel. Elkanah, however, Samuel’s father, precisely because he was not a priest, “went up,” it says, “year by year from his city Ramathaim to worship and sacrifice to the Lord Almighty of hosts; and there were Eli and his two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, priests of the Lord” (1 Sam. 1:3). What could be clearer, than that Elkanah came to offer his gifts before the Lord through the priests at the appointed time, according to what Moses had established, that three times a year they should offer their gifts and tithes in the place where the Ark of the Lord and the priests were? Especially since he had two wives at the same time, which is unlawful for priests. For Elkanah was of the Levites, as the order of generations is set forth in the book of Chronicles (1 Chron. 6:33). For at that time the Levites did not yet have a fixed order of ministry established concerning the priests and the Ark of the Lord. David, indeed, in his reign arranged courses for the priests and Levites, so that from twenty years and up, which in the Law is from twenty‑five years and up, they would begin to perform their service in the Lord’s ceremonies; and so that there should be, from the sons of Aaron, that is from the line of Phinehas and Ithamar, twenty‑four classes of priests, which would perform their courses at appointed times. The Levites, moreover, were appointed to be doorkeepers of the tabernacle, bearers of the Ark of the Lord, watchmen, keepers of the vessels, and receivers of common offerings. And twenty‑four classes of singers, harp‑players, and other musicians were established, so that these too, that is, all the Levites, would have their appointed turns in time; for it was necessary for them also to have leisure, so that they could take care of their households. And not only do these matters contribute to the above‑mentioned case, namely that Samuel was not of the sons of Aaron; but also what his mother says to the Lord: “If,” she says, “you give me a son, I will lend him to the Lord all the days of his life” (1 Sam. 1:11). She would not have said this if he were to be born a priest; he would have been obliged to serve at the altar. But because he was a Levite, and as yet no law had been laid down for the Levites, but each man acted according to his own will, so that as wanderers they presumed unlawful things, for Jonathan, the son of Moses’ son, although enrolled among the Levites, presumed to exercise the priesthood for the tribe of Dan, on this account we read in the book of Judges: “Each man did what was right in his own eyes, because there was no king in Israel” (Judg. 17:6). Therefore Hannah vowed, saying, “I will lend him to the Lord,” so that he might not wander with the rest. And so that the question may be examined more fully, let us also treat that point which is said of Elkanah, that he came year by year to offer his gifts and tithes: how did he offer tithes if he possessed nothing? For the Levites did not receive fields, since they sought their livelihood from the tithes given by the people. But it can be, and so it may be understood, that he could have had the property of his wife, or a purchased possession; for they took wives from other tribes, not only they, but others as well, so that even priests took wives from other tribes. For Jehoiada the high priest took as wife from the tribe of Judah the daughter of King Joram (2 Chron. 22:11).

(1 Samuel 15:24; 2 Samuel 12:13)

1ST CATEGORY OT

QUESTION 18. WHY IS IT THAT SAUL, WHEN HE SINNED, ASKED THAT PRAYER BE MADE FOR HIM SO THAT HE MIGHT BE FORGIVEN AND COULD NOT OBTAIN IT, WHILE DAVID, WHEN HE SINNED, ASKED AND OBTAINED PARDON? — It is not fitting that God’s judgment be revoked: for human weakness and ignorance ought to be instructed by God’s judgment in what it does not understand, so that from God’s decision it may grasp the truth, and recognize that nothing else ought to have been done than what it sees God has done, knowing that He is not a respecter of persons (Acts 10:34). For if God received David’s prayer and rejected Saul’s, we must not think that God did anything unjust. Knowing with what nature each one spoke, He accepted the petition of the one whom He saw asking for pardon with a troubled heart; but He despised the other, because the pain of repentance had not touched his soul. For God is more a hearer of the heart than of the voice. Therefore it is said, Man looks on the outward appearance, but God on the heart (1 Sam. 16:7). Therefore we too are often deceived, because hoax in words and in countenance misleads us: for we cannot see what is in the heart. Wherefore we must follow God’s judgment, who examines each person according to the heart, in which the nature of each one is found. We discover that the Savior did this as well. For He did not receive the scribe when he presented himself (Matt. 8:19); but He called Levi as he sat at the tax booth (Matt. 9:9; Luke 5:27): because the scribe’s words were not followed by the heart, whereas Levi, in silence, had in his heart what the scribe had in his words. But Jesus, who, as it is written, knew what was in man (Jn. 2:25), chose Levi. Moreover, David did not wish that another should be humbled for him as Saul did, but he himself, as a pleading with a troubled heart, asked for pardon.

 (1 Samuel 26:16) 

1ST CATEGORY OT

QUESTION 35. HOW CAN DAVID STILL CALL SAUL THE ANOINTED OF THE LORD, AND DO HIM HONOR IN THIS EXCELLENCE AFTER THE LORD HAD DEPARTED FROM HIM? — David is not unaware that there is a divine institution in the office of the royal order; therefore he honors Saul, who is still placed within that same institution, lest he seem to do injury to God, who has decreed honor for these orders. For the king bears the image of God, just as the bishop does that of Christ. As long, therefore, as he is within that institution, he is to be honored, if not for his own sake, then for the sake of the order. Therefore the Apostle says, Be subject to the higher powers. There is no power except from God; and the powers that exist are ordained by God (Rom. 13:1). From this it follows that we honor even a pagan who holds power, although he himself is unworthy, since, while holding God’s order, he gives thanks to the Devil. For authority demands honor, because it deserves it. Therefore the dream of the coming famine was revealed to Pharaoh (Gen. 41:1–37); and Nebuchadnezzar, while others stood by him, alone saw the Son of God in the fiery furnace (Dan. 3:92), not indeed by his own merit, he who wished to be adored in an idol, but by the merit of the royal order.

2 SAMUEL

(2 Samuel 28:7–20)

1ST CATEGORY OT

QUESTION 27. WHEN SAMUEL WAS SUPPOSEDLY RAISED UP BY THE PYTHONESS, AND HE WAS SEEN BY HER AND SPOKE TO SAUL—THIS STORY IS REPORTED IN THE BOOK OF KINGS? — I consider it an unworthy deed if assent is given in accordance with the wording of the story. For how could it happen that a man holy by birth and righteous by the works of his life might be drawn by magical art? Or if he was not drawn against his will, did he give consent? To believe either of these about a righteous man is absurd. For if he was brought unwillingly, his justice has no support; but if he came willingly, he lost the spiritual merit which, being in the flesh, he had sought: which is very absurd, because whoever departs from here righteous, remains righteous. Moreover, this is a trick of Satan, by which, so that he may deceive many, he even pretends to have the good in his power. The Apostle, among other things, says, “Satan himself transforms himself into an angel of light” (2 Cor. 11:14). For, in order to cause an error in which he himself might glory, he disguised himself in the guise and name of a righteous man: so that he might lie and claim that the hope proclaimed to the worshipers of God would accomplish nothing, when he pretended that the righteous going forth from here were in his power. But some are deceived by the fact that he did not lie about the death of Saul and his sons: as though it were a great thing for the Devil to foresee the day of a body’s fall beforehand, when certain signs are accustomed to appear in those who are dying, from whom the protection of God seems to have been removed. How much more the Devil, whom prophetic oracles testify to have been exalted with angelic majesty; of whose greatness the Apostle says, “Do you not know the height of Satan?” (see 2 Cor. 2:11). What wonder, then, if he was able to foresee a death that was close at hand, since this is the very thing by which he deceives and wants to be worshiped as if he were in God’s power? For Saul, made senseless by such dullness, fled to the pythoness. Corrupted by the cause of sin, he turned himself to those things which he had condemned. But if someone, on account of the story and the things expressed in words, thinks they should not be passed over, lest the logic of the narrative be empty, he will indeed do rightly, provided he does not drag this into the realm of truth, but keeps it to sight and understanding. For Saul, having become reprobate, could not have a good understanding. The narrator described Saul’s mind and Samuel’s appearance, expressing the things that were said and seen, omitting whether they were true or false. For what does he say? When he heard in what form he had been raised up, “He understood,” he says, “that this was Samuel.” He reported what Saul understood; and because he did not understand rightly, he adored someone other than God, contrary to Scripture; and thinking it was Samuel, he worshiped the Devil, so that Satan might have the fruit of his deceit. For this he strives after, that he may be worshiped as though he were God. For if Samuel had truly appeared to him, surely that righteous man would not have allowed himself to be worshiped, he who had preached that God alone is to be adored. And how could the man of God, who was with Abraham in refreshment, say to a man of disease, worthy of the burning of Gehenna, “Tomorrow you will be with me”? In these two points the unwary Satan betrayed the subtleness of his deception, both because he allowed himself to be worshiped in the guise and name of Samuel contrary to the Law, and because he falsely claimed that a man weighed down by sins, although there is a great distance between sinners and the righteous, would be with Samuel, the most righteous. In truth, it can seem reasonable if the name of Samuel is left aside, since Saul was going to be with the Devil. For he passed over to him whom he worshiped. For the Devil, always lurking under a veil, reveals himself when he invents things that clash with the persons through whom he seeks to deceive.

1 KINGS

(1 Kings 3:11)

2ND CATEGORY OT

QUESTION 18. WHY DID SOLOMON HAVE THE SPIRIT OF WISDOM (1 Kings 3), WHEN HE DID NOT HAVE A PURE LIFE? FOR HE TOOK GREAT DELIGHT IN WOMEN, AND BY THIS HE SINNED (ibid. 11). —  At first Solomon received the spirit of wisdom by his own merit; but later, when he began to make excessive use of women and thereby to sin, if he had the spirit of wisdom, he had it by reason of his royal office, just as Nebuchadnezzar, by reason of his royal office, saw Christ in the furnace.

2 KINGS

(2 Kings 2:10)

1ST CATEGORY OT

QUESTION 26. QUESTION ABOUT ELISHA: DID HE OBTAIN WHAT HE IS SAID TO HAVE ASKED TOO HARSHLY OF ELIJAH? — Elisha, eager in spirit for performing miracles and enticed by the example of his master, when he received the permission to ask for whatever he wished, greedily for good things requested that the spirit be present in him in double measure compared with what it was in his master. To him the man of God Elijah said, “You have asked a hard thing.” For in his eagerness he did not consider that the disciple is not above the master (Matt. 10:24). Yet Elijah, knowing that he had not asked this out of ambition for present glory, replied: “Nevertheless, if you see me taken from you, it shall be so for you.” (2 Kings 2:10) This meaning must be weighed carefully. Having first said with some displeasure, “You have asked a hard thing,” he added, “Yet if you see me taken up, it shall be so for you,” and therefore he did not seem to have refused him. He showed that it would be so for him as was fitting, not as he himself had requested. For Scripture intends many things to be understood completely, so that the sense gathered from the words may not be contrary to the rule of religion. Indeed, such a hard request ought in justice to have lost its reward; but because he desired the good so earnestly, God, who knows what should be given to each person, did not allow him to be deprived of the merits of his good intentions. Let us therefore see whether the merit of Elijah would allow that Elisha should deserve to receive a double portion of his gift. For it was said by the Holy Spirit through Zechariah what the merit of John would be: “He shall go,” he says, “in the spirit and power of Elijah” (Luke 1:17). He therefore shows John to be equal to Elijah. And the Lord says, “Among those born of women there has arisen no greater prophet than John the Baptist” (Matt. 11:11). He did not say, “He is greater than all,” but, “No one is greater than he”; that is, he has an equal, but he has no superior. Elijah therefore is equal to him, certainly not lesser than he; how then is Elisha greater than Elijah, when John, than whom no one is greater, is equal to Elijah? For when Elisha came to the crossing of the waters, he did not receive honor from them so as to be able to cross, unless he invoked the God of Elijah (2 Kings 2:14); so that by this his hard request might appear corrected, since he was heard only in the name of Elijah, lest he be thought to have obtained what he had asked too harshly, as though the dispensation of the Spirit granted to Elijah were not sufficient for the merit of that time.

TOBIT

1ST CATEGORY NT

QUESTION 119. ON TOBIT. — Such is the providence of the Lord God toward us that, unwilling for us to go astray, He has given both the law and examples of good works, by which life can be conducted modestly and peacefully in the fear of God. For He who is the author of life certainly does not will that His work be subject to death. Although nature itself is not without a law, yet because the Lord is good and merciful, He has shown by writings and examples, as the present reading shows, so that there might be a greater knowledge both of what must be followed and of what must be avoided. Therefore the holy servant of God, Tobit, has been given to us as an example after the law, so that we may know how those things which we read are to be carried out; and if temptations come, we may not depart from the fear of God, nor hope for help from any other than Him, remembering that it is written: I have been young, and now am old, and I have never seen the righteous man forsaken, nor his offspring begging bread (Ps. 36:25). Therefore, whoever hopes in God with his whole mind can never be deceived. Although for a time tribulations may arise through the plots of Satan, the examples of holy men teach us that these are not permitted by God except for the increase of our merits: for if they are accepted with a calm spirit, here comfort with effect will be given to us, and in the future eternal life with glory. For since our God is just, and with Him there is no respect of persons (Rom. 2:11), He allows us to be tempted because He loves us, so that after toil He may be able to bestow upon us the richest rewards. Accordingly, when the Apostle prayed that temptations might depart from him, the Lord said, My grace is sufficient for you; for strength is made perfect in weakness. Therefore the Apostle added, When I am weak, then I am strong; and he says, I rejoice in my tribulations, that the power of Christ may dwell in me (2 Cor. 12:9–10). We are taught by Scripture how praiseworthy the holy Tobit is: neither captivity diminished his devotion, nor did the loss of his eyes persuade him to cease blessing God, nor did the exhaustion of his substance turn him aside from the path of righteousness and truth (Tob. 1–3). For necessity tests the righteous man; and to preserve righteous in poverty is true and perfect righteousness. From that very source from which the devotion of some is diminished, the praiseworthy Tobit drew increase. For, it is said, poverty humbles a man; and one who is humbled cannot preserve righteousness. But the soul of the holy Tobit, lifted up toward God, was neither broken by captivity nor cast down by poverty: for even against the edict, he committed the bodies of the slain to burial, and, confident in the generosity of God, he showed mercy out of that very little he had, knowing that mercy shown from limited resources is especially pleasing to God; as also did that widow whom the Lord in the Gospel praised highly (Luke 21:2–4). For he is truly faithful, he does not doubt the promises of God, who gives from the little he has. Therefore, consoling his soul with the hope of future things, Tobit, consecrated to God, was found strong and unwavering in temptation, showing that in necessity one must be all the more watchful in the fear of God; for if necessity does not drive us to seek God’s help, how much less will security? Holy men, being certain that God has reserved to Himself the judgment of all things that happen in this world, not only bore with tribulations and losses and other disasters or insults without distress, but even accepted them gladly: as did our apostles, who rejoiced after being beaten, because they were found worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Christ (Acts 5:41). For the misfortunes that unjustly happen to the faithful, whether in tribulations or in insults, are signs of future merits. Therefore the just Tobit pleased God so greatly that by a double kind of merit he obtained his reward: for in the present life he recovered the sight he had lost through the ministry of an angel, and was enriched also with possessions pertaining to this present life; and in the future he was made an heir of the kingdom of heaven. In this we are taught that whoever obeys the law of God with all his heart and does not doubt His promises, God often increases his riches even in this world, and in the future grants him eternal life. There is also another point that invites us to divine service. For holy Tobit not only obtained rewards for his own righteousness; there is added to the fullness of his glory also the good that comes from those who become his imitators. For in imitators examples are praised. This too can happen for us, if we live in such a way that it is fitting for us also to have imitators.

(Tobit 12:7)

2ND CATEGORY OT & NT

QUESTION 8. IN TOBIT IT IS SAID: “TO REVEAL AND CONFESS THE WORK OF GOD IS HONORABLE” (Tob. 12:7). BUT THE SAVIOR, WHEN PERFORMING THE WORK OF GOD, SAYS: “TELL NO ONE” (Mark 8:26). — The Savior did not say that the work of God ought to be concealed; for elsewhere he says: “Go and tell how great things God has done for you” (Mark 5:19). Rather, he sometimes rejected their testimony and checked their boasting, lest he should appear, as would seem absurd to the wise, to be bearing witness to himself as a deceiver.

JOB

1ST CATEGORY NT

QUESTION 118. ON JOB. — Great is the love, dearest brothers, of Almighty God toward the human race: when it is understood, it leads to the heavenly kingdoms; when it is not understood, it leads down to Hades. For God wills His favor to be received with gratitude and to be fruitful, so that it may profit us and give Him delight in showing mercy. Therefore, since He is good and wills all men to be saved, He has shown us a model of righteousness in His servant Job, as the present reading bears witness, so that by following him we may both avoid evil and attain to good, and not only be freed from punishment, but also receive reward. How admirable, then, is the most holy Job, who, before the written law was given, displayed in his deeds the pattern of the Law; taking no instruction from any external teaching in this matter, but guided by nature itself, in which God decreed that the seeds of righteousness should naturally reside, he preserved reverence for his Creator through devout virtue. How great, then, is the praise he deserves, and with what words should his deeds be celebrated, since we can find no equal to him either before the Law or after the Law? For although someone might be able to imitate his achievements, he is still not to be compared with him, nor will he be rightly called his equal. It would not be his own achievement that he became such a man if he merely followed another’s example. But Saint Job, having seen nothing of the kind, nor read of it in any books, showed himself to be such that he had nothing in himself derived from another, but rather imparted to others, offering the pattern of wondrous deeds by which God might be won. Therefore he is praised by the testimony of the Lord, who says: Have you considered my servant Job? For there is no one like him on the earth, a true worshiper of God (Job 1:8). Who could have deserved so much that the Lord should bear such witness of him, unless it be this man who is found not as an imitator, but as the author of the things he did? Therefore he is proclaimed a true worshiper of God. No counterfeit impression of a fabricated truth can appear in one who has no such predecessor. Everyone who pretends, pretends to what is seen and imitated. And yet even greater things than these are said. For in these praises there were no proofs of tribulations, but only a purpose dedicated to God, established in exercise and observance. Since this did not appear to the tempter to be complete for the crown of merits, he asked that he might be allowed to test Job’s righteousness with various temptations, so that, pressed in many ways, he might somewhere be entangled and exceed due measure. For it is for this end that various punishments are usually inflicted on sinners: since no one can bear all forms of torment, one of them may wring from him a confession of the truth. Therefore the tempter was allowed to destroy and ruin all his possessions, even to the death of his sons: so that if he could bear the loss of his oxen, he might not bear that of his sheep; or if he could bear the loss of his sheep, he might not bear the loss of his camels, nor of his servants, nor of his entire substance; or if, because he was of great spirit and of pure devotion, he was not overcome by all these things, then at least he might be broken by the compelling affection of love through the immediate death of all his children. But because, before the written Law was given, he had the Law written in his heart, neither losses nor griefs made him any less devoted to God, so that he gave a pattern of loving God with all the heart above all things. How great, then, is the glory he deserves, who before the Law kept the Law, so that the Law that was to come might be shown in deeds, not words, as to how it should be observed, he being its author in action? And because the tempter is disrespectful, this glory did not seem sufficient to him for proving the righteous man, unless he manufactured something else against him which he knew could not be tolerated by a man; he asked again that he might strike Job himself with a cruel wound from the crown of his head to the nails of his feet. And when this was granted, since no trust should be placed in him, he was commanded to spare his soul for the sake of free will, and not to dare anything violent against him whom he could not overcome by right reason. Having received this power, and his cruelty raging anew within him, he struck the righteous man with a very great blow, so that there was nothing in his body that was free from injury, something no man could have endured except Job alone, who was able to conquer Satan. And when even so the hatred of the Devil could not draw from the righteous man any murmur against God, remembering his former cunning by which he deceived Adam, he strove to see if he could also deceive this man through a woman; for one is more easily deceived by someone of one’s own household. And in all these things Satan, utterly shameless, achieved nothing, indeed suffered loss: he not only found God’s servant immovable, but even his teacher. For in the very extremity of his necessity, Job not only persevered in the fear of God, but also, rebuking his wife who suggested the opposite, taught that all things which happen by God’s permission must be bravely endured (Job 2:1–10): which belongs to a double punishment of the foolish Satan, because he neither persuaded what he wished, and while envying this man, he made others learn what he did not even want this man to know. How much temptation profits the servants of God and harms the Devil we are more fully taught by this reading. For when he thinks he is harming them, he is advancing them; and when he persecutes one, he rouses many to virtue. Seeing this man protected by the helps of God, many become his imitators. Therefore, wishing to make a gain, he suffers loss. His rage is always ruinous to himself. For when he persecutes the righteous so that they may not be rewarded, he makes them more worthy; and when he envies Saint Job, he doubles his excellence in heaven and on earth; for here he is increased, and in heaven he is received with the Savior; so that all these things may contribute to the glory of the saints, and to the punishment of the Devil.

PSALMS

(Psalm 1) 

1ST CATEGORY NT

QUESTION 110. ON THE FIRST PSALM. — “Blessed is the man who has not stood in the way of sinners.” (Ps. 1:1a) But if he has stood, he is no longer blessed, but guilty and worthy of blows. For he seems to have some hope of correction, because he is not wicked, but a sinner. But if there is one who has not gone in the counsel of the wicked, and has not stood in the way of sinners, he is blessed in a twofold way. For he cannot be blessed if he does not go into the counsel of sinners yet stands in the way of sinners; for even if he is not destined for destruction, he is still accountable to punishment. Then he added, “And has not sat in the chair of pestilence.” (Ps. 1:1b) He says this is the blessedness which consists in these three steps and is guarded by this threefold rule; that is, that one neither go into the counsel of the wicked, nor stand in the way of sinners, nor sit in the chair of pestilence. But since only two kinds are mentioned, that of the wicked and that of sinners, in the record of those things just mentioned, to which class did he wish to assign this third, which he added, saying, “And has not sat in the chair of pestilence”: to that of the wicked, or of the sinners? But let us see what it is to sit in the chair of pestilence, and then we shall understand to which class he assigns this. We call that the chair of pestilence which is outside the ordering of God, clearly devised for this purpose, that unjust judgments may proceed from it. For this reason it is called the chair of pestilence, because it is a corruption that produces death, just as iniquity produces condemnation. Therefore that chair which is the chair of death is not from God. For Moses received the chair of life. It was given for this purpose, that in it there might be the authority of the just judge or of the creator God. Therefore the Lord says, “The Scribes and Pharisees sit on Moses’ chair” (Matt. 23:2); and the Apostle, “There is,” he says, “no power except from God; and those that exist are ordained by God” (Rom. 13:1). Therefore he says to the leader of the people: “You indeed sit judging according to the Law, and against the Law you order me to be struck” (Acts 23:3). When he said “according to the Law,” he indicated the just and saving authority of the chair. But in that he said “against the Law you order me to be struck,” he showed that very judge to be unjust, so that, sitting in God’s chair, he judged unjustly. Therefore also Daniel says, “The kingdom is God’s, and he will give it to whom he will” (Dan. 4:14). For just as the authority of an earthly emperor runs therefore through all, so that in all there is reverence for him, so God has ordained that from the king the authority of God should begin and run through all: although the world often does not understand this, and subjects itself to others placed in power than it ought, still the ordinance is that there should be one who is feared. Where, then, this ordinance is not, there the chair of pestilence is found. Nowhere is the authority of the one God denied except among those who proclaim fear and reverence of many gods. These, then, are those who sit in the chair of pestilence, because what their priests proclaim is death. For they deem it necessary that worshippers of the one God, as fools and enemies, should either be held up to reproach or removed from this life. This is the very material of wickedness, which also extends into other areas, through which it may display the laws of its own wickedness. For at Jezebel’s command the priests of iniquity sat in the chair of pestilence, who, against the innocent Naboth, though they were not judges, plotting stubbornness, with false witnesses corrupted, pronounced a sentence of death (1 Kings 21:11–13). Therefore also in another Psalm he says, “I will not sit with the wicked” (Ps. 25:5). For this is the judgment of him whose also is the chair of pestilence. Therefore, if, while sitting in God’s chair, they oppress the innocent, the judgment will be unjust, not the chair. For where the chair of pestilence is, the judgment cannot be other than iniquitous, even though they may attach to themselves certain coverings, as it were, by which they cloak their wickedness so that those who see are deceived. For sheer wickedness cannot be put forth by itself, because it finds no buyer; and where the law of the Devil is, if he himself is named, he is shuddered at. But as honey is mixed with poison that it may lie hidden, so too they mix certain just things into the law of the Devil, and apply to it the name of truth; yet each person’s understanding must be judged, because sometimes it shows something true in order to deceive, so that when it proclaims evil things they may be thought good. Since we have asserted that the chair of pestilence is not from the ordering of God, we also call the chair of pestilence that of those who, outside the Church or against the Church, have set up chairs for themselves. For whoever presumes what is not granted is guilty; how much more if he also corrupts the tradition of him whose seat he takes? For they disturb the order begun by the Apostle Peter and preserved up to this time through the succession of bishops in an unbroken line, claiming for themselves an order without an origin, that is, professing a body without a head; therefore it is fitting to call their seat also the chair of pestilence. Nor will it be without punishment merely because they do this under the name of God. For it is clear that they conduct their own causes under the name of God. They do not do this out of zeal for God, but wishing to defend a place for themselves. Though we know that Korah and the two hundred and fifty men, who by presumption made offerings to God, were swallowed up by the opening of the earth (Num. 16:31, 35), and that King Uzziah, when he made an unlawful offering to God, was struck with leprosy on his forehead (2 Kings 15:5 and 2 Chron. 26:21). Since it has become clear that the chair of pestilence belongs to the wickedness mentioned above, let us pursue what follows. For he added: “But his will was in the law of the Lord.” (Ps. 1:2a) He says that his will is in the law of the Lord who, despising the wicked and abandoning sinners, refusing the chair of pestilence, has fixed his will in the law of God. Therefore he called this man blessed. And it continues: “And in his law he will meditate day and night.” (Ps.1:2b) It is clear that such a man, free from all allurements and untouched by those things that are opposed to the law of God, occupies himself with nothing else than the law of God; strengthened by the sacraments of the Son of God, by day he persists in good works, and by night in prayers. For this is he of whom it is said in the Song of Songs that he sleeps and his heart keeps watch (Cant. 5:2). Therefore he says: And he shall be like a tree that is planted beside streams of water. (Ps. 1:3a) Who doubts that one who meditates on the law of God has hope of receiving the reward? For just as a tree planted beside water cannot be barren, so one who diligently studies the law of God by frequent use cannot fail to obtain the effect of his work. And he added: Which will yield its fruit in due season. (Ps. 1:3b) Every plantation that is well tended gives fruit at the proper time; so too the one who obeys the law of God will have fruit at the appointed time. For then he will receive the reward of this devotion, when the Lord Jesus Christ begins to sit in judgment of the living and the dead. Then he subjoined: And its leaf shall not fall. (Ps. 1:3c) It is clear that in a tree whose leaves do not fall, he has signified life. For a tree nourished by the moisture of running water keeps its leaves. And the Lord Jesus also says: If they do these things in the green wood, what will happen in the dry? (Luke 23:31). In the green wood he signified life and fruit. Therefore, just as a tree with the help of running water does not feel dryness, so the one who studies the law of God, when temptation approaches, remains safe by the protection of God and does not lose but gains salvation, as the Apostle says: Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God (Acts 14:21). And it continues: And all that he does shall prosper. (Ps. 1:3d) It is clear what he says, that one who keeps faith with the law of God, eager for his commandments, becomes happy in all his deeds, just like Joseph, who, because he placed the fear of God before this present life, God made all that he did prosper in his hands. And he added: Not so the wicked, not so. (Ps. 1:4a) The repetition of the phrase signifies that it will in no way turn out differently from what he promises, because nothing will be prosperous for the wicked in the future, but all things adverse, even to their destruction. Therefore he says: But like dust which the wind drives away from the face of the earth. (Ps. 1:4b) In the same way he says that the wicked perish like dust which the wind blows away from the face of the earth so that it may vanish. Once lifted away from its own substance, scattered through the air, it gradually disappears; so too the wicked, cast out by the ministering angels from the presence of God their author, without whom one cannot live, will perish. And it continues: Therefore the wicked shall not rise in the judgment. (Ps. 1:5a) What he says is fitting. For why should those rise in the judgment who chose to believe that no business of God was entrusted to them for which they would have to render an account? Since they spurned and denied the law of God, there is nothing from which they might produce an account, so as, when questioned in the judgment according to the law entrusted to them, to present their case. Therefore, found to be arrogant and rebellious against God, they rise only to see that what they refused to believe is true, so that they may perish, because they judged God to be a liar. And he added: Nor sinners in the council of the righteous. (Ps.1:5b) In this psalm the Psalmist denotes three kinds of men: the wicked, sinners, and the just, in the order in which the error began. But the wicked are strangers to these, because, as I said, they refused to live under the decree of God. Sinners, however, who act under the law of God, are to stand before the tribunal of Christ, separated from the righteous, so that they may render an account of the commandments of the law they received, in which they did not labor, so that they may have more praise than blame. The righteous, however, found to be very zealous in the exercise of fulfilling the law, are to be rewarded. And he added: For the Lord knows the way of the righteous. (Ps.1:6a) God is said to know these who, mindful of his precepts, persist in good works so that, counted as righteous, they may be crowned. But to those who, forgetful of him, are negligent about the care of their soul, he will say: Depart from me; I do not know you, workers of iniquity (Luke 13:27). And it continues: And the way of the wicked shall perish. (Ps.1:6b) Therefore the psalm is begun and ended so that, when the case of the wicked is treated, they may be shown to be accountable to nothing other than destruction. For, as I have said, God is therefore said to know the way of the righteous because they walk in his law; but the way of the wicked, because it is outside the law of God, shall perish. For all the ways of the wicked are dark (Prov. 4:19), as Solomon says, but those of the virtuous are very bright, with Christ our Lord as their guide.

1ST CATEGORY OT

2ND CATEGORY OT

(Psalm 31:9) 

QUESTION 38. IF A HORSE AND A MULE DO NOT HAVE UNDERSTANDING, HOW MUCH LESS SO DOES THE EARTH, A THING WITHOUT SENSATION? WHAT THEN DOES IT MEAN WHEN THE EARTH IS SAID TO BLESS THE LORD (Ps. 31:9; Dan. 3:74)? — It is not to be understood in the way the words sound. For a work, although it is mute, is said to cry out the praise of its Creator: for it urges those who look upon it to bless the Maker; just as every well‑crafted vessel praises the craftsperson. Indeed, when it is read in the Psalms, Shall the dust give thanks to you, or declare your truth? (Ps. 29:10) Therefore, in every insensible substance, it is not the will, of which there is certainly none, but the works that bless the author. But if you wish to take this spiritually, understand that man is signified by “earth,” according to the saying of the prophet: Remember, O Lord, that we are dust (Ps. 102:14); he whom the works of creation exhort to burst forth in praise of his Maker.

(Psalm 31:9) 

QUESTION 16. IF A HORSE AND A MULE DO NOT HAVE UNDERSTANDING, HOW MUCH LESS SO DOES THE EARTH, A THING WITHOUT SENSATION? WHAT THEN DOES IT MEAN WHEN THE EARTH IS SAID TO BLESS THE LORD (Ps. 31:9; Dan. 3:74)? — Let the earth bless the Lord, he says; that is, let it praise and confess your truth. How then in the Psalms does he say, Shall the dust give thanks to you, or declare your truth? (Ps. 29:10) It is not to be understood simply as it is read and as the words sound. For the earth does not have understanding, that it might give thanks to the Creator. But if you take this spiritually, understand “earth” as man, according to the saying of the prophet, Remember, O Lord, that we are dust. (Ps. 102:14) The work of the created world urges him to burst forth into praise of the Creator, so that he may gain the confession of His truth through those things which, although silent, are said to cry out the praise of the Creator, whose work they are. This, then, is the reason why, in the creation, the earth is said to bless God.

(Psalm 19:4; 40) 

2ND CATEGORY OT

QUESTION 17. HE HAS, HE SAYS, SET UP HIS TABERNACLE IN THE SUN (Ps. 18:6), THAT IS, HIS BODY IN WHICH CHRIST DWELT, WHO WAS SCOURGED BY PILATE: HOW THEN IS IT SAID IN THE PSALM OF CHRIST, THE SCOURGE SHALL NOT COME NEAR YOUR TENT (Ps. 90:10)? SINCE HE CALLED HIS BODY A TEMPLE. — The body of the Son of Man and of the Son of God is understood to be a temple. Yet God, that is, the Son of God, although he came in the flesh, dwelt nonetheless in the soul. Therefore both soul and body are the tabernacle of the Son of God, although there is one God and man, the Son of God and the son of man. Therefore from this standpoint it is said that the scourge did not come near his tabernacle; that is, his soul, in which his divinity dwells, was free from the punishment of hell or its rulers. Lest anyone think that because here he was crucified as if a sinner, though he is innocent, and the flesh suffered, his soul suffered some sorrow in the lower regions, Scripture shows that his soul could not be disturbed in hell, because he descended there for this very purpose, that is, he allowed himself to suffer, so that he might put the darkness to shame and render its rulers powerless. Hence the Lord himself says: My soul is sorrowful even unto death (Matt. 26:38). It was allowed, as belonged to its nature, to be sorrowful, immediately bearing off the trophy, and the spoils of those by whom it had been saddened even unto death, after death now established in eternal joy. It can also be understood of the whole man; for he who knew no sin could not be scourged by the law.

(Psalm 23) 

1ST CATEGORY NT

QUESTION 111. ON PSALM 23. — The title of the Psalm hints at its meaning. For, about to speak of the mystery of Christ our Lord, he marked the Lord’s day, saying: For David, on the first day of the week. For when it is said, For David, it relates to the one of whom this David bears the image, of whom the prophet says: And my servant David shall pasture them (Ezek. 37:24). Now the “first of the sabbath” is the first weekday. For after the sabbath the first day is the Lord’s day, as the Gospel affirms, saying: Now on the first of the sabbath Mary Magdalene and the other Mary came to the tomb, etc. (Matt. 28:1). On the Lord’s day he signified the mystery of the Savior. But so that the Psalm might be expounded according to the order of reason, he began from the person of God the Father, so that the mystery of the divinity might not be revealed to men without order. For whoever wants to lay out some case, unless he grasps its head and origin, will not be able to show its proper nature or teach what its truth is. And so the Prophet began therefore and said: The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness. (Ps. 23:1a) He preserved the truth of things by saying: The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness. For he followed the authority of the ancient saints, who said that the earth and the things that are in it belong to the Lord God. And he added: The world and all who dwell in it. (Ps. 23:1b) Lest perhaps it be thought that he had signified something less when he said, The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness, he revealed his meaning by saying, the world and all who dwell in it, so that he might teach that absolutely all the earth is the Lord’s, and the things that are in it, so that nothing should be excepted that is not God’s. As some heretics think, who, according to the saying of the apostle Peter, deny dominion to God (2 Pet. 2:10), about whom the prophetic oracles have taught that all things belong to God for condemnation. And it continues, He has founded it upon the seas; (Ps. 23:2a) that is what he expressed in another psalm, saying, You formed the earth upon the waters (Ps. 135:6): so that testimony might follow faith, he shows how he made it. For while there was confusion of things, and neither earth nor water had its own distinct form, at God’s command the earth was gathered together and fixed upon the waters, so that both earth and water might have the proper character of their origin. Therefore in the book of Kings there is the voice of God saying, Did I not make the waters? And he added: And he prepared it upon the rivers. (Ps. 23:2b) Therefore it is prepared upon the rivers, since it contains within itself stored waters, which, flowing as though through the pipes of veins, give it solidity, lest it be completely dry, fragile, and useless for cultivation. For they grant a vital effect to the roots of growing things, and at the same time they are a help against thirst in dry places. And to show that profession without a good life does not profit greatly, he says: Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord, or who shall stand in his holy place? (Psalm 23:3-4) He sets forth what sort of person one must be who professes God as creator, lest, because he has shown that those who, as I said, deny God’s dominion are to be punished, those who confess him should think themselves free from punishment if they do not live rightly. By the mountain of the Lord he means heaven. Therefore in another psalm he says: I have lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from where help will come to me (Ps. 120:1). The place of the Lord is where he appears. It is said to Joshua son of Nun, when the Lord had appeared to him, The place on which you stand is holy ground (Josh. 5:16); and Jacob, where he saw God, said, This is the house of God (Gen. 28:17). And it continues: Innocent of hands and pure of heart. (Ps. 23:4b) This person he calls worthy to ascend the mountain of the Lord, that is, into heaven, or to stand in his holy place, if someone is innocent in works and has a pure heart in the cause of God, that is, of faith. A person of this kind can ascend into heaven and stand in his holy place. For when he departs from this life he ascends into heaven. Then, when the city Jerusalem descends from heaven at the coming of the Lord, he will be worthy to stand where the Lord is going to judge the living and the dead as one who is innocent; but the ungodly and sinners will be unworthy to stand in the holy place of God’s judgment, because the ungodly will rise to destruction, sinners to punishment. For if the sons of Israel, because of sin, could not bear to look upon the glorified face of Moses when he came down from the mountain (Ex. 34:29–30), how much more will a conscience burdened by sins dread to behold the Lord himself of glory sitting on the throne of his majesty? For they will hear, I do not know you, workers of iniquity (Matt. 7:23). And he added: Who has not taken his soul in vain. (Ps. 23:4c) Now he touches on the very kinds of sins. First of all, in this place, he is innocent and has a pure heart, who is free from the fornication of idolatry. For this is vanity itself, and whoever bends himself to it brings his soul into bondage to corruption. And it continues: Nor has sworn deceitfully to his neighbor. He has mentioned two causes, which are principal: those of God and of neighbor; because whoever is found upright in these will without doubt be approved in other matters also, as the Lord says, You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your strength. This is the first commandment. And the second is like it, You shall love your neighbor as yourself. On these two commandments hang the whole Law and the Prophets (Matt. 22:37–40). Who then, loving God with all his heart, would not keep his law? Or who, having love for his neighbor, would strive after sins? since it is because of fear of God that he loves his neighbor. And he added: He shall receive blessing from the Lord, and mercy from God his Savior. (Ps. 23:5) Now he shows what is the reward of one who has had faith and love in the cause of God and man, of the creator and of neighbor: that he will both be blessed by the Lord, so that he may appear praised, and will obtain mercy in those things which he has not been able to fulfill. For no one can be so watchful as never to err at all; but because he is found zealous and faithful in great matters, he may also receive mercy from his God in lesser ones. He is therefore called Savior, because he does not will the death of one who is dying, but that he should turn back and live (Ezek. 18:32). And it continues: This is the generation of those who seek the Lord, who seek the face of the God of Jacob. (Ps. 23:6) He has said there is one generation of those who seek God, and of those who seek the face of the God of Jacob, and this is not idle. For although both are good, yet by these words he has indicated two degrees. It is a good thing to seek God; it is a fullness of good to seek the face of the God of Jacob. For those are more worthy who are before the face of the judge. Of these merits, therefore, this is the generation: because innocence and purity of heart bring one to this point; just as, in turn, if one is to come to evil, unrighteousness and iniquity go before. For there are two generations: one on the side of iniquity, which is the mother of Cain; the other on the side of righteousness, which is the mother of Abel: the latter consists in faith and good conduct; the former in treachery and crooked works. These are the two laws, of good and of evil, of God and of the Devil; and whichever one a person has followed, he will be called its son. And therefore this is the generation of those who seek God: faith in God and love for neighbor, as we have said above. For whoever has faith in God is always seeking his help; nor does he show himself unjust to men who wishes to have God as his gracious protector. The sign of this is when he is called the God of Jacob, because God is known in Judah (Ps. 75:2). But why are they said to seek his face, when Moses heard, For, he says, my face shall not be seen by you (Ex. 33:20)? If therefore even Moses sought the face of God and could not see it, then these are said to seek in vain, because they are not better than Moses. But no one should be said to seek the face of God in vain, because they are therefore said to seek the face of God so that it may be known whom they seek, since they are worthy also to see him. For everyone who is sought is then known if his face is seen. But since the face of God cannot be seen by mortals, this expression stands for “face” when it is said, the God of Jacob. Diapsalma. In this passage Diapsalma signifies a change of person. For after those things which pertain to the person of God the Father, he adds those which pertain to the mystery of God the Son, so that the full order of Father and Son is preserved. For the Law was given through Moses so that it might be as an instructor for men, instructing and preparing them as a teacher of righteousness, so that they might become worthy of the year of the Lord’s expiation and the day of recompense; so that those who under the hope of the future Christ had been faithful might receive him and be able to escape Adam’s sin, being secure regarding their own, because his coming, which they had hoped for, would grant them mercy concerning those things in which it slipped upon them so that they sinned. This is what he mentioned above, saying, He shall receive mercy from God his savior. He therefore says: Lift up your gates, you princes. (Ps. 23:7a) This is the voice of the holy angels, of whom he says in the Gospel that, he says, angels came and ministered to him (Matt. 4:11). These then speak to the princes and powers against whom the Apostle says we have our wrestling (Eph. 6:12), that they should lift up the gates of their prince, that is, of the Devil, who is the prince of princes set in error, through which one goes into Gehenna. These gates are unbelief and the deceit of idolatry. And it continues: And be lifted up, you everlasting gates. (Ps. 23:7b) Faith and hope with love are everlasting gates, because what is proclaimed through truth cannot be abolished. But those gates which I said are unbelief and the deceit of idols are temporal, because no lie remains. For when the truth is revealed, it will perish. They are therefore taught to take away the gates of their prince of darkness, that is, that with the error of many gods removed, the faith of the one God may be brought in, in Christ. This is what the Apostle testifies that he was sent to teach, that he might show not only to men, but to princes and powers in the heavenly places the mystery of the one God in Christ (Eph. 3:8–12). And he added: And the king of glory shall enter. (Ps. 23:7c) He commands that the deceitful gates, subtly fashioned by the Devil, be taken away, these are presumption, through which he thought himself a god, so that the king of glory may enter, who is Christ Jesus our Lord. For faith in God enters no one’s mind unless he has removed from himself the error invented by the Devil’s transgression. And the princes mentioned above cannot receive Christ the king into the faith of the one God unless they cast from themselves the tradition by which slander is brought upon the one God; not only the earthly slander, but also that which in heavenly places has been seized by the prince of princes, Satan. For the error which they conspired among themselves, so that at the Devil’s instigation they called themselves gods, they also arranged here on earth, so that this error might be its image here. And it continues: Who is this king of glory? (Ps. 23:8) Lest it might perhaps be thought that Christ was called king of glory unnecessarily, he introduces the person of one asking and saying, Who is this king of glory? As though he were in amazement or wished to be taught whether it is true and fitting to call Christ king of glory. And therefore they answered him: The Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle, so that by this being added he might learn Christ to be king of glory, not by basic words but with testimony. For the strength and power by which he subdued and crushed the Devil with his attendants show him to be the king of glory. And he added: Lift up your gates, you princes, and be lifted up, you everlasting gates; (Ps. 23:9a) that is, since by the testimony of his power, which it is wicked to contradict, you have learned that it is worthy that Christ be called king of glory, remove error from your minds. And in that he says, The king of glory shall enter, it is shown that they cannot share in the faith of Christ unless they have cleansed their hearts from all impurity of idolatry. For unless man has been renewed, the Holy Spirit will not enter him. And it continues: Who is this king of glory? (Ps. 23:9b)  This repetition brings confirmation. For everything that is heard as new is not grasped in the heart unless it is repeated. And it brings wonder and astonishment when that which has never been heard before is spoken. And he added: The Lord of hosts, he is the king of glory. (Ps. 23:10) By repeating the same, he teaches that it is rightly said that this one is king of glory, who is the Lord of hosts. For he is not undeservedly called king of glory who rules over the powers. Where the Apostle: For if they had understood, he says, they would never have crucified the Lord of majesty (1 Cor. 2:8).

(Psalm 35:7) 

2ND CATEGORY OT & NT

QUESTION 7. WHAT DOES IT MEAN IN THE PSALM, “MEN,” HE SAYS, “AND BEASTS YOU WILL SAVE” (Ps. 35:7); AND IN THE PROPHET JONAH, “I WILL NOT SPARE,” HE SAYS, “THE CITY IN WHICH LIVE ONE HUNDRED AND THIRTY THOUSAND PEOPLE, AND MANY ANIMALS” (Jonah 4:11); WHEREAS THE APOSTLE SAYS, “DOES GOD CARE FOR OXEN?” (1 Cor. 9:9). — As far as the wording goes, it seems contradictory; but if the purpose of man and of animals is considered, it will become clear that it is not different. God takes care of all, as the maker of all; but he does not preserve animals for their own sake, he preserves animals for the sake of men, not men for the sake of animals. Therefore, in caring for men, he keeps the animals, so that his concern is not for oxen, but for human beings. For what hope is there in animals?

(Psalm 39; 50) 

2ND CATEGORY OT

QUESTION 12. WHY IS IT THAT IN THE LAW EVEN AARON HIMSELF IS TOLD THAT HE MUST OFFER BURNT OFFERINGS FOR HIS SINS, WHEN DAVID SAYS, “FOR FAULTS YOU HAVE NOT REQUIRED A BURNT OFFERING” (Ps. 39:7), AND LATER, “YOU WILL NOT TAKE PLEASURE IN BURNT OFFERINGS” (Ps. 50:18)? HOW DID HE COMMAND THAT THERE BE OFFERED WHAT HE DOES NOT TAKE PLEASURE IN? — It is clear that God does not take delight in burnt offerings, but that by way of satisfaction for sin, through the groaning and sorrow of the heart, pardon can be earned. He willed that the sacrifice should be a testimony of sin, so that the sinner, by the offering of the sacrifice, might confess that he had sinned. But how forgiveness might be obtained, He showed in another place, saying, “Break your bread for the hungry; if you see one naked, clothe him, and do not despise your own flesh and blood” (Isa. 58:7), or certainly, “A contrite and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise” (Ps. 50:19). First, then, He instructed that the offense must be confessed; then He showed how it can be forgiven. For He never commanded a sacrifice for an obvious, clear offense, but for sins of ignorance; because even when a man does not know, he sins, and when he thinks he is acting rightly, by a certain intention he goes astray. Such a sin, He said, can be cleansed by a sacrifice.

(Psalm 39:16) 

2ND CATEGORY OT & NT

QUESTION 6. WHAT DOES IT MEAN WHEN DAVID SAYS, “LET THEM BE CONFUSED AND ASHAMED WHO SAY TO ME, ‘WELL DONE, WELL DONE’” (Ps. 69:4), WHILE THE LORD SAYS, “WELL DONE, GOOD AND FAITHFUL SERVANT” (Matt. 25:21, 23), ETC.? THAT WHICH DAVID TOOK AS SOMETHING BAD, THE SAVIOR SHOWS TO BE WORTHY OF GOOD MERITS. — This does not differ much from the previous question. For one and the same word has different meanings, as I mentioned above1. For the detractors of David, since they supported his destruction, were rejoicing at his misfortunes. While he was suffering pressures and distresses from Saul and from his son Absalom, they said that this was rightly and well done to him. It is like when someone says, of a man who is suffering wrongs, “It serves him right”; that is, to rejoice in another’s troubles: this is to say, “He is getting what he deserves.” In a similar way, the Savior, rejoicing in good works, proclaims a man’s merit by saying, “Well done, good and faithful servant.” For he exults because the servant has made himself more worthy, saying, “Well done,” that is, “You have acted rightly, so that you might place yourself in a position of greater merit.” Therefore one word is applied to two opposite causes. For we are accustomed to say of someone, “He has been judged.” But how it is said is made clear by the cause that either follows or precedes. For sometimes it is said with reference to good, sometimes to evil; just as desire is sometimes directed to good, sometimes to evil.

1 In the second part of the New Testament questions, question 54.

(Psalm 50) 

1ST CATEGORY NT

QUESTION 112. ON PSALM FIFTY. — The Fiftieth Psalm is placed here not according in chronological order, but according to rationale. For its title is governed not by number, but by meaning. As far as history is concerned, it comes before the third. For the prophet Nathan rebuked him for his sin before his son Absalom rose up against him to deprive him of both life and kingdom. This is therefore the reason why the Fiftieth is placed here, as is evident from the Law. For there it is established that the number fifty carries remission. It comes after seven weeks and is the first that bears the type of the Lord’s Day: because just as after seven days, the first day is that which was made at the beginning, and which, after each completed week, is always the first; so also, after seven weeks, the fiftieth, when counted, is in mystery the first, and is called in a double sense the Lord’s Day: first, because it was made at the beginning by the Lord, and, always recurring upon the completion of the weekly cycle, is the first; then, because on it the Lord rose again, having triumphed over death, it is also called the Lord’s Day. Not without reason, then, in the number fifty, which we observe as mystically signifying the first, remission is contained. Indeed, the Law was given on the fiftieth day. For from the departure of the children of Israel out of Egypt, they were commanded on the forty-eighth day to be washed, so that, purified for two days, on the third day they might be ready to receive the Law (Exod. 19:10, 11). And what else does that washing indicate but that remission was granted on the fiftieth day, so that, purified, they might receive the Law? From that point on, with past things blotted out, they should render an account of their conduct according to the Law entrusted to them. For this same reason the Law also commanded that a purchased possession be restored in the fiftieth year (Levit. 25:10). From this, therefore, comes the title of the Fiftieth Psalm. In it King David asks for remission according to this prefigured meaning; therefore he says: Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy. (Ps. 50:1a) Knowing that he had sinned gravely, King David therefore asks, saying: Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy. For mercy is great when great sins are forgiven. And he adds: And according to the multitude of your tender mercies, blot out my iniquity. (Ps. 50:1b) To make clear that he had sinned grievously, he calls his sin “iniquity,” because iniquity is no light fault; and he who blots out iniquity, that is, does not credit it, abounds in mercy. He therefore tries in no way to excuse himself in his case, so that he may not only soften the mind of the Judge toward him, but also move Him to compassion. For the mind is stirred to mercy when it sees the accused confess his sins in such a way as to show that he is grieved because he has sinned. For whoever does not grieve seems to mock the judge; for he prays only to escape, meaning to commit the same again. And he continues: Wash me thoroughly, he says, from my injustice, and cleanse me from my sin. (Ps. 50:2) Since he proclaims the abundant mercy of God, he begs to be cleansed completely, so that nothing of fault or injustice may remain in him that could cause suspicion. And that he might obtain or secure this very thing, he adds: For I know my iniquity, and my sin is always before me. (Ps. 50:3) Because he knows that he has sinned grievously, he is anxious lest it be not entirely forgiven him. Considering the greatness of his sins, he fears, knowing that grave sins are not easily forgiven; and therefore he confesses with tears, keeping his sin before his eyes, in order in every way to make the Judge merciful toward him. For he knows it is written: Declare your iniquities first, that you may be justified (Isa. 43:26). And he continues: Against you alone have I sinned, and done evil before you. (Ps. 50:4a) Now, from another angle, he provides a remedy for his fault, so as to bring his petition to its effect. By this line of argument he declares himself innocent in the primary matter: for whoever sins against another god is an enemy of the God who is Creator. For he chooses another in place of Him, to whom he attributes His authority. Therefore, showing that he is free from such iniquity, he says: Against you alone have I sinned, and done evil before you; (Ps. 50:4b) that is, because I have sinned against you, and not against any other whom through error I might call god, my guilt is less than that of others, who are subject to punishment. For I am not wicked, but a sinner, because I have not sinned against you yourself, but against your Law; nor have I denied you, but, confessing you as God and Lord, I have sinned against a man. Therefore, since in that which is your own proper cause I am not guilty, forgive what I have done against a fellow-servant. For therefore I have sinned that I neither denied the honor of your name nor gave it to another. There was therefore reason for the Judge to be moved to mercy. For although many sin against Him, whom He even urges to turn back to Him, yet when those who do not sin directly against Him nevertheless ask pardon for other reasons, He readily receives them. For the Lord always wills His servants to flee to His help. Therefore he adds: That you may be justified in your words, and prevail when you are judged. (Ps. 50:4c) While asking for mercy, he prays that God may not change His justice, since justice is ordinarily a middle course such that it is not equal toward those who do not sin and those who do, that is, that it renders to each according to his works; but the innocent man in the mystery of God does not fail to understand what he asks. For knowing that God has frequently said in the Law, For I am merciful, says the Lord your God (Exod. 22:27), from there he begs that this faith may remain firm, and that God may be justified in His words, by remaining in what He has spoken, and not be overcome by the sins of men so as not to show mercy. For those who sin, knowing what God has promised to those who live well, and that He perseveres in this, judge Him to be a liar. For by living badly they do not believe that what He promised is true. Therefore King David asks that God may overcome this opinion men entertain, and may give what He has promised, so that those who, not keeping the commandments, judge that He will not give, may be put to shame. And he continues: Behold, I was conceived in iniquities. (Ps. 50:5) Now, with this added, he recalls the cause of the weakness of the human race, namely that it is easy for man to sin, so that he might soften the severity of the judgment upon himself. For he makes mention of the first fault, by which Adam, through transgression, made the human race subject to sin. Under the persuasion and deceit of the enemy, conceiving iniquity, he subjected all his offspring to iniquity, so that all born from him by breeding should be liable to sin. Therefore he added, “And in sins my mother conceived me,” (Ps. 50:5b) so that the transmission of sin from Adam would be an obstacle for those conceived and born, hindering them from living a good life; and therefore mercy should not be denied to the suppliant, since he has a hostile enemy who urges him to sin. For through sin the Devil, having subjected the first man to himself, received power to mingle with his flesh and, with a certain restraint of offenses, suggest pleasures, by which he strips captive man of life. Remembering this, the teacher of the Gentiles says: “I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind” (Rom. 7:23); so that, seeing this, the Judge may stretch out his hand to one in sorrow and under assault. And it continues: “Behold, you have loved truth.” (Ps. 50:6a) Because you love truth, he says, come to the aid of the one who prays, the one whom you know lays bare the true impairments of his heart, and to every guilty person you once, moved by mercy, decreed to give help, so that the error committed on earth might be corrected by heavenly providence. For this reason he adds: “You have made known to me the uncertain and hidden things of the heart.” (Ps. 50:6b) By “uncertain and hidden things of the heart” he means those things which God has provided for the protection of the human race, just as the Apostle says: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, the things that God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Cor. 2:9). Who are those who love God, if not those who consent to his law, neither hiding nor excusing sins? These “hidden things of the heart” are revealed to those who love God, so that, because they grieved at being overwhelmed by sins, they might not deny it when corrected, crediting it both to themselves and to their origin, and not transferring to God as author the things they did in sin. Their hearts were illumined by spiritual brightness, so that they might see God’s providence in Christ, namely that he was going to come to condemn the sin which, from Adam’s transgression, ruled over the human race. This, then, King David prays for: that what God had decreed for the future, seeing the human race toil, he might first grant to himself, constrained by the same necessity in which he had decreed to help all; so that the gift which was to be free and could not be given before the time, might, to him, be granted in advance for his prayer and tears. He does not remain silent about how this is to happen, saying: “You will sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed.” (Ps. 50:7a) Rightly does he ask to be cleansed by the sprinkling of hyssop. For with this the sons of Israel smeared their doorposts with blood, that they might be kept safe from death (Exod. 12:22–23); so here too he prays by the sprinkling of hyssop to be cleansed from his sins, lest he be touched by death. And it continues: “You will wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow.” (Ps. 50:7b) Clearly, God’s work differs from man’s work: therefore he says, “I shall be whiter than snow,” because what God has done is much better than what man has done. For this reason he asks to be cleansed by the sprinkling of hyssop, so that as the bodily flesh is washed with water, in the same way, through the signification of hyssop, the stains of souls may be washed away by spiritual means. For the sprinkling of hyssop is a kind of purification, so that by means of what is visible, one may be cleansed invisibly. And it continues: “You will give joy and gladness to my hearing.” (Ps. 50:8a) There is no doubt that the voice of one proclaiming forgiveness brings joy to sinners. For who does not rejoice when he hears that pardon is being granted? For when God forgives, he is safe both in the present and the future. “And the bones that have been humbled shall rejoice.” (Ps. 50:8b) There is a twofold sense in which the bones are humbled: both in that he was humbled so that he might sin, for no one who sins is exalted, and in that afterward he, as a suppliant, might beg pardon. For he certainly, rolling in sackcloth and ashes, begged for mercy; which, once obtained, he was raised up in the exultation of his mind and the restoration of his body. And he added: “Turn your face away from my sins, and blot out all my iniquities.” (Ps. 50:9) With this form of words he asks for forgiveness, just as it was established for the future through faith in Christ, that the Savior, who is promised to him spiritually, should begin with him to grant all sins to those who are converted.
